playground.label: Scope and errors (uses input)

findings: Chapter 4 of the 3rd edition teaches functions: the def statement that defines one and the call that runs it, arguments passed into parameters, return values and the None value, named parameters such as print's sep and end, the call stack that remembers where each call returns to, the local and the global scope and four rules for telling them apart, the global statement, and try and except for recovering from an error, closing with two short animation programs.

One printed output of the chapter has changed: it shows UnboundLocalError: local variable 'eggs' referenced before assignment, while Python 3.14.4 says cannot access local variable 'eggs' where it is not associated with a value, the wording the Programming FAQ now prints; the class, its parent NameError and the cause are unchanged, and the chapter's other printed error messages, NameError and ZeroDivisionError, are the same under 3.14.4.

The chapter's copy-and-paste listing, which it shows to argue for functions, is not equivalent to the function version it stands for: its last line is print(' Good evening!') with a leading space, so running the two programs gives outputs that differ in exactly that line - which is the maintenance hazard of duplicated code the passage warns about.

The reference documentation explains why the chapter's fourth scope rule and its UnboundLocalError follow from one fact: which names are local is decided by scanning the whole function body for name-binding operations, so an assignment anywhere in a function makes the name local everywhere in it; the standard library's symtable module shows the decision - the same name eggs is global in a function with a global statement, local in one that assigns it, and global in one that only reads it.

The chapter's call-stack example reproduces line for line, and the stack itself can be looked at from the program: the standard library's traceback module lists the frames a call is running inside, and the interpreter refuses to grow the stack without end - the recursion limit is 1000 and a function that calls itself forever raises RecursionError, a subclass of RuntimeError, rather than crashing.

For an advanced course, chapter 4 is best taught as name resolution seen from the function: a call creates a scope, the compiler decides which names in it are local, the call stack holds the scopes that are waiting, and try and except decide where in that stack an error is handled; the book's rules are the four cases of one lookup rule, the printed messages should be regenerated under the Python in use, and parameters, defaults, nonlocal, annotations and the 3.14 except syntax are what the chapter leaves for the course to add.

Beyond the chapter, a function's parameters can be positional-only, with a slash, or keyword-only, with a star, and calling them the wrong way raises a TypeError that names the problem; a default argument value is evaluated once, so a mutable default such as an empty list is shared between calls and the tutorial's remedy is a default of None; and nonlocal lets an inner function rebind a name of the enclosing function, the middle case between local and global that the chapter does not cover.

Python 3.14 changed two things a course on functions meets: annotations on a function are no longer evaluated when it is defined, so a function annotated with names that do not exist yet can be defined and called, and reading its annotations raises NameError until they are evaluated on request; and except may list several exception types without brackets when no as clause is used, which 3.13 and earlier reject.

The chapter text names tools and ideas that the earlier corpus did not explain: reserved keywords, the lambda expression, the nested function, the function taken from a module, the positional argument, the frame object and stack inspection, recursion, namespaces and the lookup of names, the symbol table, the nonlocal statement, the exception object, the traceback, the exception hierarchy, the time.sleep function, the KeyboardInterrupt exception, the sys.exit function, the two practice programs, function annotations, function naming and comments. The Python glossary defines the namespace, the nested scope, the lambda, the keyword argument and the positional argument; the language reference gives the function definition, the try statement and the lambda expression, the call, and the function object, the frame object and NoneType; the library documentation covers traceback, inspect, symtable, time, random, keyword, the constant None and annotationlib; the tutorial introduction defines the comment; PEP 3107 defines function annotations and PEP 8 gives the conventions for names and comments. Every output and error message quoted was executed under Python 3.12.11 and 3.14.4, and the messages that differ between releases - division by zero, the empty range of randint, the unexpected keyword of print, the except clause without brackets, deferred annotations and the annotation blocks in the symbol table - are pinned to their release in the corpus and never quoted as stable. Two statements of the chapter do not hold when run: its hint to print the Collatz values with sep puts each value on its own line, and its claim that the sequence reaches 1 for any integer fails for 0 and for -1.
title: Functions for an advanced course

nodes.label: Function
nodes.body: A function is a named piece of code that a program can run whenever it needs that work done, from as many places as it likes. The textbook describes it as a mini program within a program (Sweigart, 2025), and the Python glossary states the same idea more formally: a series of statements which returns some value to a caller, and which can also be passed zero or more arguments that are used while its body runs (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The values passed in are called arguments, and the code that runs is called the body; both terms are defined carefully in the sections that follow.

paras.text: A function is a named piece of code that a program can run whenever it needs that work done, from as many places as it likes. The textbook describes it as a mini program within a program (Sweigart, 2025), and the Python glossary states the same idea more formally: a series of statements which returns some value to a caller, and which can also be passed zero or more arguments that are used while its body runs (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The values passed in are called arguments, and the code that runs is called the body; both terms are defined carefully in the sections that follow.

Without functions, every task that a program repeats would have to be written out again at each place that needs it, and a correction would have to be made in every copy. A function lets the programmer give the task a name, write it once and use the name from then on. The chapter adds a second reason: the variables created inside a function stay inside it, so a function can do its work and interact with the rest of the program only through the values it receives and the value it gives back, which narrows down the lines of code that can be responsible when something goes wrong (Sweigart, 2025).

Functions are already familiar from chapter 1, where print, input and len were used as built-in functions that Python provides ready to use. This chapter shows how to write new ones with the def statement, how to call them, how to pass values in and get a value out, and what happens in the computer while one function waits for another to finish. Everything a Python program does beyond a few lines is organised into functions, whether the author wrote them or imported them from a module.

The chapter is easiest to follow in the order of its own sections. Creating and calling a function comes first, then the two ways of passing values in (as parameters and as arguments), then the return value that comes out and the special value None. After that the call stack explains how Python finds its way back from a call, the scope rules explain which variable a name refers to inside and outside a function, and exception handling explains how a program can recover when a function fails. Two short animation programs and a note on current Python close the material.

Two ideas that sound alike must be kept apart: the function itself, which is created once by a def statement, and a function call, which is each occasion on which that function runs. The practice questions of the chapter ask for exactly this difference (Sweigart, 2025), and most of the confusing error messages in the sections ahead come from mixing the two up.

nodes.label: Definition
nodes.body: The definition branch covers how a function is created and how it is run. A function is created by a def statement, which names the function and gives it a body; it is run by a function call, which names the function again and supplies any arguments (Sweigart, 2025). Between the two lies a function object, the thing Python actually builds when it meets the def statement.

paras.text: The definition branch covers how a function is created and how it is run. A function is created by a def statement, which names the function and gives it a body; it is run by a function call, which names the function again and supplies any arguments (Sweigart, 2025). Between the two lies a function object, the thing Python actually builds when it meets the def statement.

Almost every misunderstanding about functions can be traced to the gap between defining and calling. A learner who keeps the two moments apart can predict when the code in a body runs, in what order a program prints its lines, and why a function must exist before the line that calls it executes.

The sections of this branch go from the statement to the object to the call, and then to the reason for all of it. The def statement, the body, the function object and the keyword def come first, followed by the call, the call of a function that lives in a module, the lambda expression as a short way of writing a small function, and the function written inside another function. The branch ends with deduplication, the practical benefit that the textbook uses to justify functions.

The gap between the two moments can be measured. The body does not run when the def statement is met: Python builds a function object, binds it to the name and moves on, so a file whose only statement is a def prints nothing at all. The object can then be examined, since a function named double answers double.__name__ with the string double and double.__code__.co_argcount with 1 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Calling the function from a line that runs before its def statement raises NameError, because the name is bound when that statement executes and not when the file is read.

nodes.label: Def statement
nodes.body: A def statement is the construct with which a Python program creates a function of its own. It is written with the keyword def, the name chosen for the function, a pair of parentheses and a colon, and it is followed by an indented block of statements that forms the body. The textbook introduces it with a function named hello that prints three greetings (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A def statement is the construct with which a Python program creates a function of its own. It is written with the keyword def, the name chosen for the function, a pair of parentheses and a colon, and it is followed by an indented block of statements that forms the body. The textbook introduces it with a function named hello that prints three greetings (Sweigart, 2025).

Without def, a program could use only the functions that Python already provides. With it, the programmer names a piece of work once and every place that needs the work can use the name. The language reference calls a function definition an executable statement, which means that the function comes into existence at the moment the program reaches the def line and not before (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A def statement is found near the top of nearly every program that is longer than a few lines, usually above the code that calls the function. It can be typed in a file or in the interactive shell, and it can also appear inside the body of another function, which makes a nested function.

When execution reaches a def statement, Python builds a function object and binds the function's name to it in the current namespace. It does not run the body; the reference states that the function definition does not execute the function body, which is executed only when the function is called (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that defines hello with a print inside and then runs print('before') prints only the word before, because the greeting inside hello is never asked for.

A function must be defined before the line that calls it runs. A program whose first line is hello() and which defines hello underneath stops with NameError: name 'hello' is not defined, because at that moment the def statement below has not been executed yet. The colon at the end of the def line and the indented body under it are both required, and the next section on the function body explains the error that follows when the body is missing.

nodes.definition: A def statement creates a function and binds its name; the body runs when the function is called, not when it is defined.

nodes.label: Function body
nodes.body: The body of a function is the block of indented statements that follows the colon of the def line. The textbook puts it directly: the code in the block that follows the def statement is the body of the function (Sweigart, 2025). The body is the description of what the function does, and the def line is the description of what it is called and what it expects.

paras.text: The body of a function is the block of indented statements that follows the colon of the def line. The textbook puts it directly: the code in the block that follows the def statement is the body of the function (Sweigart, 2025). The body is the description of what the function does, and the def line is the description of what it is called and what it expects.

Python has no braces and no closing keyword to mark where a function stops, so the indentation is the only boundary. A line that is indented under the def line belongs to the function, and the first line that returns to the left margin belongs to the code that follows. Reading the indentation correctly is therefore the first step in reading any function.

Every function has a body, and the body can contain any statement from the earlier chapters: calls to print, assignments, if statements with their elif and else parts, and loops. It can also contain a return statement, which ends the call, and further def statements, which create functions inside the function.

The body is not executed when the function is defined. Each time the function is called, Python starts at the first line of the body and runs downward until it reaches the end of the block or a return statement, and then the execution continues on the line after the call (Sweigart, 2025). Variables that the body creates belong to that one call and disappear when it ends. A body must contain at least one statement; the statement pass does nothing and exists for the case in which a statement is required but no action is, such as a placeholder for a function that is still to be written (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A def line followed by no indented line, or by a line that is not indented, stops the program with IndentationError: expected an indented block after function definition on line 1. Equally easy to miss is a line that is indented by mistake: a statement meant to run once after the function but typed at the body's indentation becomes part of the body and runs only when the function is called.

nodes.definition: The block of indented statements after the colon of the def line; it runs on each call, from its first line to the end or to a return statement.

nodes.label: Function object
nodes.body: A function object is the value that Python builds when it executes a def statement. The language reference describes the execution of the statement as binding the function name in the current local namespace to a function object, a wrapper around the executable code for the function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The name hello is therefore only a label, and the function itself is the object that the label refers to.

paras.text: A function object is the value that Python builds when it executes a def statement. The language reference describes the execution of the statement as binding the function name in the current local namespace to a function object, a wrapper around the executable code for the function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The name hello is therefore only a label, and the function itself is the object that the label refers to.

Seeing a function as an object explains behaviour that would otherwise look arbitrary. The name can be copied to another name, passed to other functions, or reused for something else, because a function is a value like the numbers and strings of chapter 1. The reference makes the same point when it says that functions are first-class objects, which can be returned or passed around (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The object is visible whenever a function is named without being called. The call type(hello).__name__ gives 'function', callable(hello) gives True, and after same = hello the test same is hello is also True, because both names refer to one object. The same test works on a built-in function: callable(len) is also True. A built-in function such as len is reported as a built-in function or method instead, since it was not made by a def statement.

The tutorial puts it plainly: a function definition associates the function name with the function object in the current symbol table, and other names can also point to that same function object and be used to access the function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function object also carries information about itself; its name is stored under the attribute __name__, an attribute being a named piece of information that is attached to an object and reached with a dot.

Because the name is only a label, assigning to it replaces the function. After def hello(): and then hello = 5, the call hello() stops with TypeError: 'int' object is not callable. Writing the bare name hello with no parentheses does not call anything; it only refers to the object, so the line has no visible effect.

nodes.definition: What a def statement actually creates: a value of type function, which the function's name refers to and which can be given other names.

nodes.label: Reserved keyword
nodes.body: A keyword is a word that has a fixed meaning in the Python language, which is why it cannot be chosen as the name of a variable or function. The words def, return, global, nonlocal, try and except that this chapter introduces are all keywords. The standard module keyword lists them in keyword.kwlist and tests a word with keyword.iskeyword (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A keyword is a word that has a fixed meaning in the Python language, which is why it cannot be chosen as the name of a variable or function. The words def, return, global, nonlocal, try and except that this chapter introduces are all keywords. The standard module keyword lists them in keyword.kwlist and tests a word with keyword.iskeyword (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A learner meets keywords as the words that start statements. Knowing that they are reserved explains an error message that would otherwise be puzzling: a program that tries to use def as a variable name, as in def = 3, stops with SyntaxError: invalid syntax, because the word already means something else.

The textbook mentions keywords only to dismiss a confusion. It says that named parameters, which it also calls keyword arguments, have nothing to do with Python keywords (Sweigart, 2025). The word keyword in keyword argument means that the argument is given with the name of a parameter; the word keyword in def or return means a reserved word of the language.

Whether a word is a keyword is a fixed fact about the language, and the keyword module can answer it. print is not on the list: keyword.iskeyword('print') is False, because print is a built-in function that can be given a new meaning, while def, return, global, nonlocal, try and except are all in keyword.kwlist and keyword.iskeyword('None') is True. The style guide adds that when a parameter name would clash with a keyword, a single trailing underscore is better than an abbreviation, so class_ is preferred to clss (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

Do not confuse a keyword with a built-in name. A built-in name such as len can be reassigned by accident, which silently hides the function, whereas a keyword cannot be reassigned at all. The two situations produce different errors, and the section on the built-in scope returns to the first.

nodes.example: def, return, global, nonlocal, try, except
nodes.definition: A word that has a fixed meaning in the Python language and cannot be used as a name; def, return, global, nonlocal, try and except are keywords.

nodes.label: Lambda expression
nodes.body: A lambda expression creates a small function in the middle of another expression. The glossary calls it an anonymous inline function consisting of a single expression which is evaluated when the function is called, written as lambda parameters: expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The expression lambda a, b: a + b therefore stands for a function that receives two values and gives back their sum.

paras.text: A lambda expression creates a small function in the middle of another expression. The glossary calls it an anonymous inline function consisting of a single expression which is evaluated when the function is called, written as lambda parameters: expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The expression lambda a, b: a + b therefore stands for a function that receives two values and gives back their sum.

A def statement needs a name and several lines, which is more than a one-line calculation deserves when the function is used only once. A lambda expression can be written exactly where the function is needed. This course uses it mainly in examples, where it keeps a demonstration of parameters or return values to a single line that can be typed into the interactive shell.

The expression (lambda a, b: a + b)(2, 3) evaluates to 5: the first pair of parentheses holds the function and the second pair calls it with two arguments. The language reference explains that the expression is shorthand for a simplified function definition and behaves like a def of a function named <lambda> whose body is a return statement (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The body of a lambda is one expression and nothing else. The reference states that functions created with lambda expressions cannot contain statements or annotations, so lambda: pass is rejected with SyntaxError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The result is an ordinary function object, which has the name <lambda> instead of a name chosen by the programmer.

The style guide advises against binding a lambda to a name with an assignment such as f = lambda x: 2*x and recommends a def statement, because the def form gives the function the name f instead of the generic <lambda> that appears in tracebacks and string representations (Van Rossum et al., 2001). In the program that assigns the lambda to add, add.__name__ is '<lambda>' while a def function called add2 reports 'add2'.

nodes.definition: A way to write a small function as a single expression; it has no name of its own and its body is one expression.

nodes.label: Nested function
nodes.body: A nested function is a function that is defined inside the body of another function. The reference notes that a def statement executed inside a function definition defines a local function that can be returned or passed around, and that such a function can use the local variables of the function containing the def (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A nested function is a function that is defined inside the body of another function. The reference notes that a def statement executed inside a function definition defines a local function that can be returned or passed around, and that such a function can use the local variables of the function containing the def (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Nested functions let a helper stay next to the only code that needs it, without adding another name to the whole program. They also lead to the case of the scope rules that sits between a purely local and a purely global variable: a variable of the outer function, which the inner function can read and, with the nonlocal statement, can change.

A small helper that is meaningful only inside one function is a typical nested function, and so is any function that builds and returns another function. Most beginner programs do not need them, but the nonlocal statement of this chapter and the lookup rule for names cannot be understood without them.

Executing the outer function runs the inner def statement each time, so the inner function object is created anew on every call of the outer one. In the program that defines outer with a variable n set to 21 and an inner function that returns n * 2, calling outer() prints 42. Because the inner name is local to the outer function, using inner after outer has returned raises NameError: name 'inner' is not defined.

Defining a function inside another one does not run it. The inner function runs only when it is called, and the outer function has to call it or hand it on. A nested function can read the variables of the outer function freely, but an assignment inside it creates a new local variable instead of changing the outer one, which is the reason the nonlocal statement exists.

nodes.definition: A function defined inside the body of another function; it exists only while the outer function runs and can read the outer function's variables.

nodes.label: Function call
nodes.body: A function call is the function's name followed by parentheses, with the arguments, if there are any, written between them. The textbook states that when the program execution reaches such a call it will jump to the first line in the function and begin executing the code there (Sweigart, 2025). The same notation was used in chapter 1 to call print, input and len.

paras.text: A function call is the function's name followed by parentheses, with the arguments, if there are any, written between them. The textbook states that when the program execution reaches such a call it will jump to the first line in the function and begin executing the code there (Sweigart, 2025). The same notation was used in chapter 1 to call print, input and len.

A call is what makes a function do any work, because a definition alone runs nothing. It is also an expression: a call such as max(3, 7) evaluates to the value the function gives back, so it can be used wherever a value can, which later sections develop.

Calls are the commonest construct in a program. The program in the textbook calls hello three times and prints ten lines, three greetings, the line ONE MORE TIME! and three greetings again (Sweigart, 2025). Calls to the functions of modules are written with the module's name and a dot in front, and the next section shows that form.

The reference describes the order of events: every argument expression is evaluated before the call is attempted, and the thing being called must be a callable object, a function being the usual case (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Python then places the arguments into the parameters, runs the body, and returns to the line after the call when the body ends or a return statement is reached (Sweigart, 2025).

The parentheses are what make it a call. A line that contains only hello does nothing visible, as the section on the function object shows. The number of arguments must also fit the definition: calling a function defined as hello() with one argument, as in hello('Alice'), stops with TypeError: hello() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given.

nodes.definition: A call is the function's name followed by parentheses, with any arguments inside, and execution jumps into the body and comes back.

nodes.label: Module function
nodes.body: A module function is a function that is defined in a module and used after importing that module. The chapter's fortune-telling program imports the module random and then calls random.randint(1, 9), whose two arguments are the smallest and the largest number that may come back (Sweigart, 2025). A module, as chapter 1 explained, is an object that serves as an organisational unit of Python code.

paras.text: A module function is a function that is defined in a module and used after importing that module. The chapter's fortune-telling program imports the module random and then calls random.randint(1, 9), whose two arguments are the smallest and the largest number that may come back (Sweigart, 2025). A module, as chapter 1 explained, is an object that serves as an organisational unit of Python code.

Most of the usefulness of Python lies in functions that other people have already written and placed in modules. The glossary notes that writing random.seed() makes it clear which module implements the function, and that the module's namespace prevents two functions with the same name from colliding (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The library documentation defines random.randint(a, b) as returning a random integer N such that a <= N <= b (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The call random.randint(5, 5) therefore always gives 5, and random.randint(1, 9) gives a number from 1 to 9 inclusive, which is how the fortune program picks one of its nine answers.

The import statement of chapter 3 binds the module's name in the current namespace; the dotted name then looks up the function inside that module. Without the import line, the name random is simply undefined, and a program that calls random.randint(1, 6) first stops with NameError: name 'random' is not defined.

Arguments given in the wrong order matter here, as they do everywhere. The textbook points out that random.randint(1, 10) is different from random.randint(10, 1): the first gives a random integer between 1 and 10 and the second causes an error (Sweigart, 2025). Running the second form under Python 3.12 and 3.14 raises ValueError in both, although the wording of its message differs between the two releases.

nodes.definition: A function that lives in a module is called with the module's name and a dot in front, after the module has been imported.

nodes.label: Deduplication
nodes.body: Deduplication means getting rid of copied-and-pasted code, and the chapter names it as a major purpose of functions. The textbook explains that without a function you would have to copy and paste the code each time you wanted to run it, and that deduplication makes programs shorter, easier to read and easier to update (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Deduplication means getting rid of copied-and-pasted code, and the chapter names it as a major purpose of functions. The textbook explains that without a function you would have to copy and paste the code each time you wanted to run it, and that deduplication makes programs shorter, easier to read and easier to update (Sweigart, 2025).

Copies drift apart. If a bug is found in code that was pasted three times, the textbook warns, you must remember to change every place where you copied it. A function turns the three copies into one body and three short calls, so a correction is made once and is seen by every call.

The chapter demonstrates the point with the greeting program. The version with a function has the three greetings written once and called three times; the pasted version spells out every print line, which makes it ten lines of print instead of four. Counting in the two sources, the text Good evening! occurs once in the function version and three times in the pasted version.

The chapter's own pasted listing contains an example of the hazard it warns against. Its last line is print(' Good evening!') with a space before the G, so running the two programs gives outputs that differ in exactly that line: the function version prints Good evening! and the pasted version prints a line that begins with a space. Both outputs have ten lines, so the difference is easy to overlook, which is precisely the risk of duplicated code.

A function is not the answer to every repetition. If the same few lines differ slightly each time, the differences should become parameters, which the next branch explains; if the repetition is a loop over the same steps, a loop from chapter 3 may be simpler than a function.

nodes.definition: A function groups code that runs more than once, so a fix is made in one place instead of in every pasted copy.

nodes.label: Parameters
nodes.body: Parameters are the way values get into a function. A function definition lists the names that will receive the values, and each call supplies the values themselves. The textbook covers the plain form first, in the sections on arguments and parameters, and then the form in which an argument is identified by name, in the section on named parameters (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Parameters are the way values get into a function. A function definition lists the names that will receive the values, and each call supplies the values themselves. The textbook covers the plain form first, in the sections on arguments and parameters, and then the form in which an argument is identified by name, in the section on named parameters (Sweigart, 2025).

A function that always did exactly the same thing would be of limited use. Parameters let one body serve many situations, such as greeting any person by name or dividing 42 by any number, so that the function stays short while the calls differ. They are also the controlled doorway through which a function receives information, because a function's own variables cannot be seen from outside.

The branch begins with the vocabulary of define, call, pass, argument and parameter, then separates the two ways of matching an argument to a parameter, by position and by name. It continues with the two ways of forcing one of them, the slash that makes parameters positional-only and the star that makes them keyword-only, and ends with default values, which let a call omit an argument. The tutorial summarises the whole family in one definition line, def f(pos1, pos2, /, pos_or_kwd, *, kwd1, kwd2), where each marker restricts how the arguments that follow it may be passed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The matching rules can be broken in three ways, and each has a message of its own. Passing more arguments than the definition accepts raises a TypeError naming the function and the two counts; supplying one parameter twice, once by position and once by name, raises a TypeError saying that the function got multiple values for that argument; and placing a positional argument after a keyword argument is refused before the program starts, with SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A parameter with a default may simply be left out, and the remaining rule is that no parameter without a default may follow one that has one.

nodes.label: Parameter and argument
nodes.body: An argument is a value that is passed to a function in a call, and a parameter is the variable in the function definition that receives it. The textbook defines the pair with one example: in def say_hello_to(name) the name is a parameter, and in the call say_hello_to('Al') the string 'Al' is an argument that is assigned to the parameter (Sweigart, 2025). The glossary agrees that an argument is a value passed to a function when calling it and that a parameter is a named entity in a function definition that specifies an argument the function can accept (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An argument is a value that is passed to a function in a call, and a parameter is the variable in the function definition that receives it. The textbook defines the pair with one example: in def say_hello_to(name) the name is a parameter, and in the call say_hello_to('Al') the string 'Al' is an argument that is assigned to the parameter (Sweigart, 2025). The glossary agrees that an argument is a value passed to a function when calling it and that a parameter is a named entity in a function definition that specifies an argument the function can accept (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The two words are used constantly in documentation, error messages and conversation, and they name two different things that are easy to swap. Using them correctly is what lets a learner read a sentence such as the third argument is not accepted by the second parameter without hesitation, and it is what the textbook means when it says that keeping these terms straight ensures that you know precisely what the text means (Sweigart, 2025).

Every call in this chapter has both. The call say_hello_to('Alice') passes one argument, and the function prints three greetings that begin Good morning, Alice and end with Good evening, Alice; a second call with 'Bob' prints three more lines for Bob. The built-in call round(3.14159, 2) passes two arguments, the number and the digits to keep, and evaluates to 3.14.

The textbook lists four verbs: to define a function is to create it, as an assignment statement like spam = 42 creates the spam variable, to call it is to send the execution to the top of its code, and to pass a value is to hand it to the function in the call. The arguments are then assigned to local variables called parameters (Sweigart, 2025). The reference adds that a function call always assigns values to all parameters mentioned in the parameter list, whether from positional arguments, from keyword arguments or from default values (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A parameter lives only as long as the call. The textbook points out that the value stored in a parameter is forgotten when the function returns, so print(name) after say_hello_to('Bob') stops with NameError: name 'name' is not defined (Sweigart, 2025). The number of arguments must also match the parameters: calling say_hello_to() with none stops with TypeError: say_hello_to() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'.

nodes.definition: An argument is the value passed in a call, a parameter is the variable that receives it, and the parameter is forgotten when the function returns.

nodes.label: Positional argument
nodes.body: A positional argument is an argument that Python matches to a parameter by its place in the call: the first argument goes to the first parameter, the second to the second, and so on. The glossary defines it negatively but precisely, as an argument that is not a keyword argument, one that appears at the beginning of an argument list (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook states the rule in its section on named parameters: Python identifies most arguments by their position in the function call (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A positional argument is an argument that Python matches to a parameter by its place in the call: the first argument goes to the first parameter, the second to the second, and so on. The glossary defines it negatively but precisely, as an argument that is not a keyword argument, one that appears at the beginning of an argument list (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook states the rule in its section on named parameters: Python identifies most arguments by their position in the function call (Sweigart, 2025).

Position is the shortest way to write a call, and it is the form every function accepts unless its definition restricts it. It also means that the order of the arguments is part of the meaning of the call, so a learner who ignores the order will get wrong results or errors without any warning.

The built-in divmod takes two numbers and returns a pair consisting of their quotient and remainder under integer division, which for integers is the same as (a // b, a % b) (Python Software Foundation, 2026); the two operators were introduced in chapter 1. divmod(7, 2) gives (3, 1), while the same two numbers in the other order, divmod(2, 7), give (0, 2), and divmod(17, 5) gives (3, 2). The textbook's own example is random.randint(1, 10), which is different from random.randint(10, 1) (Sweigart, 2025).

The language reference describes the matching as a list of unfilled slots, one for each formal parameter: if there are N positional arguments, they are placed in the first N slots, and only then are keyword arguments assigned to slots by name (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A slot that receives two values raises TypeError, and a slot that is never filled and has no default value also raises TypeError.

A positional argument may not follow a keyword argument in a call. The tutorial states that in a function call, keyword arguments must follow positional arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and a call such as print('a', sep=',', 'b') is rejected before the program runs, with SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument.

nodes.definition: An argument matched to a parameter by its position in the call, so swapping two arguments changes the result.

nodes.label: Named parameter
nodes.body: A named parameter is a parameter whose argument is identified by the name written before it in the call, as in sep=',', and not by its position. The textbook adds that you will also hear named parameters called keyword parameters or keyword arguments, though they have nothing to do with Python keywords (Sweigart, 2025). The tutorial gives the general form kwarg=value and notes that keyword parameters are also referred to as named parameters (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A named parameter is a parameter whose argument is identified by the name written before it in the call, as in sep=',', and not by its position. The textbook adds that you will also hear named parameters called keyword parameters or keyword arguments, though they have nothing to do with Python keywords (Sweigart, 2025). The tutorial gives the general form kwarg=value and notes that keyword parameters are also referred to as named parameters (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Names make a call readable and let optional values be left out. The textbook says that programmers often use named parameters to provide optional arguments, and the clearest case is print: it has the optional parameters end and sep, which choose what is printed at the end of its output and between its arguments (Sweigart, 2025). A reader who sees end='' knows what it means without opening the documentation.

Without any naming, print('Hello') followed by print('World') puts the two words on separate lines, because print adds a newline character at the end. With print('Hello', end='') the first call prints nothing at its end, so the output is HelloWorld on one line. The call print('cats', 'dogs', 'mice') prints cats dogs mice with spaces between the words, and adding sep=',' prints cats,dogs,mice. The coin-flip program of the textbook uses end=' ' so that the H and T results appear on one compact line, and two such calls followed by a bare print() give the line H T with a space after the T.

The library reference defines print with the parameters sep, whose default is a single space, end, whose default is a newline, file and flush, and adds that sep, end, file and flush, if present, must be given as keyword arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In an ordinary function, a parameter can be matched either way, so int('ff', base=16) and int('ff', 16) both give 255. When both a positional and a keyword argument try to fill the same parameter, as in f(0, a=0), the call stops with TypeError: f() got multiple values for argument 'a' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A name that the function does not know is an error: print('a', separator=',') raises TypeError, and the wording of the message differs between Python 3.12 and 3.14. Because sep, end, file and flush are keyword-only in print, writing the separator as a plain extra argument does not set it; print('cats', 'dogs', ',') simply prints the comma as a third word, giving cats dogs , with spaces.

nodes.definition: A named parameter is identified by its name in the call rather than its position; print's sep and end are two.

nodes.label: Positional-only parameter
nodes.body: A positional-only parameter is a parameter that can receive its argument only by position and never by name. It is marked by placing a slash in the parameter list: every parameter before the slash is positional-only. The glossary gives the same definition, with def func(posonly1, posonly2, /, positional_or_keyword) as its example (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A positional-only parameter is a parameter that can receive its argument only by position and never by name. It is marked by placing a slash in the parameter list: every parameter before the slash is positional-only. The glossary gives the same definition, with def func(posonly1, posonly2, /, positional_or_keyword) as its example (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

PEP 570 states the starting point: positional-only parameters have no externally usable name (Hastings et al., 2018). The tutorial's guidance lists the situations in which they fit: when parameter names have no real meaning, when the order of the arguments should be enforced, and, for an API (application programming interface, the set of functions that a library offers to other programs), to prevent breaking changes if the parameter's name is modified in the future (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Many built-in functions work this way. The call len(obj='abc') stops with TypeError: len() takes no keyword arguments, because the argument of len cannot be given by name. The reference notes that in CPython this is true of functions implemented in C that do not give their positional parameters names (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

For a function defined as def f(a, /, b): return a * b, the call f(3, 4) and the call f(3, b=4) both give 12, because b may be passed either way. The call f(a=3, b=4) stops with TypeError: f() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'a', which names the parameter that was misused. The worked example of this concept writes the same function as a lambda expression, which the section on lambda expressions explains.

The slash separates parameters by how they may be passed, not by which ones are required. Everything before it is positional-only and everything after it, unless a star follows, can be passed either way. Introducing a slash into an existing function breaks any caller that used the name, so it is normally chosen when the function is first written.

nodes.definition: Parameters before a slash can only be passed by position; passing one by name raises a TypeError.

error.out: TypeError: <lambda>() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'a'

nodes.label: Keyword-only parameter
nodes.body: A keyword-only parameter is a parameter that can receive its argument only by name. It is marked by a star in the parameter list: every parameter after the bare star is keyword-only. PEP 3102 introduced the idea as arguments that can only be supplied by keyword and which will never be automatically filled in by a positional argument (Talin, 2006).

paras.text: A keyword-only parameter is a parameter that can receive its argument only by name. It is marked by a star in the parameter list: every parameter after the bare star is keyword-only. PEP 3102 introduced the idea as arguments that can only be supplied by keyword and which will never be automatically filled in by a positional argument (Talin, 2006).

Requiring the name makes a call self-explanatory and removes a whole class of mistakes. The tutorial recommends keyword-only parameters when names have meaning and the function definition is more understandable by being explicit with names, or when users should be prevented from relying on the position of an argument (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The built-in print is the example learners meet first: its documentation states that sep, end, file and flush must be given as keyword arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the textbook's examples this is why the separator and the end string are always written with their names.

For a function defined as def f(a, *, b=2): return a + b, the call f(1, b=5) gives 6 and the call f(1) gives 3, because b has the default value 2. The call f(1, 5) stops with TypeError: f() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given, since the second value has no positional slot to fill.

A star must come before the keyword-only parameters, and the keyword-only parameters are not required to have a default value: for def f(*, b), the call f(b=1) works and the call f() stops with TypeError: f() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'b'. The slash and the star can be combined in one definition, with positional-only parameters before the slash, keyword-only ones after the star and ordinary parameters between them (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: Parameters after a star can only be passed by name, so a call cannot get them wrong by position.

error.out: TypeError: <lambda>() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given

nodes.label: Default argument
nodes.body: A default argument value is a value written in the definition, as in def greet(name, greeting='Hello'), which Python uses when a call leaves that argument out. The reference says that a parameter written as parameter = expression gives the function default parameter values and that the corresponding argument may then be omitted from a call (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A default argument value is a value written in the definition, as in def greet(name, greeting='Hello'), which Python uses when a call leaves that argument out. The reference says that a parameter written as parameter = expression gives the function default parameter values and that the corresponding argument may then be omitted from a call (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Defaults make the common case short and the unusual case possible. The call greet('Ada') returns Hello, Ada, greet('Ada', 'Hi') returns Hi, Ada and greet('Ada', greeting='Hey') returns Hey, Ada, so one function serves three styles of call. This is how the optional sep and end of print work.

Defaults appear in the signatures of many library functions, and in the functions a program defines itself whenever a setting nearly always has the same value. The language also requires an order: if a parameter has a default value, all following parameters up to the star must also have one, and def bad(a=1, b) is rejected with SyntaxError: parameter without a default follows parameter with a default (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The default expression is evaluated once, when the def statement is executed, and the same value is then used for each call. The tutorial's example sets i = 5, defines def f(arg=i), then sets i = 6; calling f() still returns 5 and f(7) returns 7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For the common values of chapter 1 this is invisible, but it matters when the default is a mutable object, an object that can be changed in place, such as a list.

A list is an ordered collection of values that chapter 6 introduces. A default of def f(a, L=[]) that appends to L makes the one list be shared by all calls, so the calls f(1), f(2) and f(3) print [1], then [1, 2], then [1, 2, 3] (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial's remedy is a default of None that the function replaces with a new list when it is None, after which g(1) and g(2) print [1] and [2] separately. The test is written with is, which the section on identity explains.

nodes.definition: A default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so a mutable default is shared between calls; the tutorial's remedy is a default of None.

nodes.label: Result
nodes.body: The result of a function is what a call evaluates to once the body has finished. In everyday speech a function gives something back; in Python terms the call is replaced, inside the expression that contains it, by the function's return value. The textbook introduces the idea with a familiar case: when len is called with 'Hello', the call evaluates to the integer 5, and in general the value to which a function call evaluates is called the return value of the function (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The result of a function is what a call evaluates to once the body has finished. In everyday speech a function gives something back; in Python terms the call is replaced, inside the expression that contains it, by the function's return value. The textbook introduces the idea with a familiar case: when len is called with 'Hello', the call evaluates to the integer 5, and in general the value to which a function call evaluates is called the return value of the function (Sweigart, 2025).

Parameters bring information into a function and the result carries information out. Together they make a function a small machine with inputs and an output, and this is what allows one function to be built on the results of another. A function that gives nothing back can still be useful for what it does, such as printing, but it cannot take part in a calculation.

The branch has two parts. The first, about the return value, covers the return statement, the value that Python supplies when a function has no return statement, and the use of a call as an expression. The second, about the None value, covers the special value that stands for no value at all and the way to test for it.

A function chooses its result with a return statement. If it never reaches one, Python supplies None. Either way the call can then be stored in a variable, printed, passed on as an argument or combined with operators, since a call evaluates to its return value.

nodes.label: Return value
nodes.body: The return value is the value that a function call evaluates to. It is produced by the function's return statement or, when there is none, by the value None that Python supplies. The three sections of this branch follow that order: the statement that chooses the value, the value supplied when no statement is written, and the use of the call itself as an expression.

paras.text: The return value is the value that a function call evaluates to. It is produced by the function's return statement or, when there is none, by the value None that Python supplies. The three sections of this branch follow that order: the statement that chooses the value, the value supplied when no statement is written, and the use of the call itself as an expression.

Understanding the return value separates two things that beginners often mix up, printing a result and returning it. A function that prints can only be read by a person, while a function that returns can be used by the rest of the program in arithmetic, comparisons and further calls.

The reference puts the rule in one sentence: return leaves the current function call with the expression list, or None, as return value (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Everything else in the branch is a consequence of that sentence.

Two consequences of that single sentence are worth stating plainly. A return statement ends the call at once, so a line written after it in the same block never runs, and a return with several expressions still gives back one value, a tuple, which is why a function appears to return two numbers and a call can unpack them into two names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that prints instead of returning evaluates to None, so adding two such calls raises a TypeError about NoneType rather than adding the numbers that appeared on the screen.

nodes.label: Return statement
nodes.body: A return statement ends a function call and chooses the value that the call evaluates to. The textbook says that it consists of the return keyword and the value or expression that the function should return (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference gives the same rule in its own words: if an expression list is present it is evaluated, else None is substituted, and return leaves the current function call with it as the return value (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A return statement ends a function call and chooses the value that the call evaluates to. The textbook says that it consists of the return keyword and the value or expression that the function should return (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference gives the same rule in its own words: if an expression list is present it is evaluated, else None is substituted, and return leaves the current function call with it as the return value (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Without return, a function could only act on the outside world, for example by printing. With it, a function can compute something and hand it to the caller, which is how most of the functions in a real program are used. The textbook's fortune program is a typical case: get_answer receives a number and returns one of nine strings, and the main program prints the string it receives (Sweigart, 2025).

The chapter's divide function is the simplest example. After def spam(divide_by): return 42 / divide_by, the calls spam(2), spam(12) and spam(1) evaluate to 21.0, 3.5 and 42.0, and spam(2) + spam(12) evaluates to 24.5, because the calls are values and can be added. In the fortune function, get_answer(1) returns 'It is certain' and get_answer(9) returns 'Very doubtful'.

Executing return does two things at once: it computes the value and it leaves the function immediately. In a function whose first statement is return 'first' and whose second is print('never printed'), the call returns 'first' and nothing is printed, because the second statement is never reached. The program then continues at the line that made the call, and the call is replaced by the value.

A return statement can appear several times, but only one of them is executed per call. In get_answer the nine return statements sit in an if and elif chain, and each call reaches exactly one; if no branch matches, as for get_answer(10), the function finishes without a return and the call evaluates to None. Any statement placed after a return in the same block can never run, as the print('never printed') example shows.

nodes.definition: A return statement leaves the function with the value of its expression, so a call can be used wherever a value can.

nodes.label: Implicit None
nodes.body: A function that never executes a return statement with a value still returns something: it returns None. The tutorial answers an objection that people from other languages raise, that such a function is a procedure and not a function, by stating that even functions without a return statement do return a value, albeit a rather boring one, and that this value is called None (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook describes it from the inside: behind the scenes Python adds return None to the end of any function definition with no return statement (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A function that never executes a return statement with a value still returns something: it returns None. The tutorial answers an objection that people from other languages raise, that such a function is a procedure and not a function, by stating that even functions without a return statement do return a value, albeit a rather boring one, and that this value is called None (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook describes it from the inside: behind the scenes Python adds return None to the end of any function definition with no return statement (Sweigart, 2025).

Every call evaluates to a value, so every function must have some return value, and None is the choice that means nothing useful. It is the reason print can be used in an expression at all: the textbook explains that print displays text and does not need to return anything, but since all function calls need to evaluate to a return value, print returns None (Sweigart, 2025).

The case appears whenever a function only performs an action, such as printing, and in every function whose last branch forgets to return. The tutorial's rule has two parts: a return without an expression argument returns None, and falling off the end of a function also returns None (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook also mentions that functions return None if you use a return statement without a value, that is, just the return keyword by itself (Sweigart, 2025).

For def f(): pass and def g(): return the calls f() and g() both evaluate to None, and type(f()).__name__ gives 'NoneType'. The same is true of def add(a, b): a + b, which computes the sum and throws it away: add(2, 3) is None. The rule holds for built-in functions and methods too: [2, 1].sort() is None is True, because sorting a list in place hands nothing back. The interpreter normally suppresses None when it is the only value to be written, so in the interactive shell nothing appears after a call that returns it, but print(f()) writes it.

A missing return is one of the most frequent mistakes in beginners' programs. The symptom is a calculation that seems to work but delivers None, followed by an error when None is added to a number or compared with one. When a function is supposed to give a value back, check that every path through it ends in a return.

nodes.definition: A function without a return statement, or with a bare return, returns None.

nodes.label: Call as expression
nodes.body: Using a call as an expression means putting a function call wherever a value is expected, for instance inside the parentheses of another call. The textbook notes that because you can pass return values as arguments to other function calls, the three lines r = random.randint(1, 9), fortune = get_answer(r) and print(fortune) can be shortened to the single equivalent line print(get_answer(random.randint(1, 9))) (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Using a call as an expression means putting a function call wherever a value is expected, for instance inside the parentheses of another call. The textbook notes that because you can pass return values as arguments to other function calls, the three lines r = random.randint(1, 9), fortune = get_answer(r) and print(fortune) can be shortened to the single equivalent line print(get_answer(random.randint(1, 9))) (Sweigart, 2025).

The principle behind the shortcut is the definition of an expression from chapter 1. The textbook reminds the reader that expressions consist of values and operators, and that you can use a function call in an expression because the call evaluates to its return value (Sweigart, 2025). A call is therefore just another value-producing piece of code, and it can be combined with every other one.

Nested calls are read from the inside out. In len(str(42 / 2)), the division is evaluated first and gives 21.0, the call str turns it into the text '21.0', and len counts four characters, so the whole expression evaluates to 4. Calls also take part in arithmetic, as spam(2) + spam(12) does when it evaluates to 24.5.

The language reference states the order: all argument expressions are evaluated before the call is attempted (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In print(get_answer(random.randint(1, 9))), Python first calls random.randint, passes its result to get_answer, passes that result to print and finally prints it. Each inner call has returned before the next outer call begins.

Long nested calls are short to write but harder to debug, because no intermediate value is stored where it can be inspected. When a nested line does not behave, split it back into separate assignments as in the textbook's three-line version and print each stage.

nodes.definition: Because a call evaluates to its return value, a call can be used as an argument of another call or as an operand in a larger expression.

nodes.label: NoneType
nodes.body: NoneType is the data type of the single value None. The branch explains the value and the right way to test for it. Both points matter in this chapter because None is what every function returns when it has nothing else to give back.

paras.text: NoneType is the data type of the single value None. The branch explains the value and the right way to test for it. Both points matter in this chapter because None is what every function returns when it has nothing else to give back.

A language needs a way to say that there is no value, distinct from every real value including zero and the empty string. Python uses None for this, where other languages use null, nil or undefined, as the textbook mentions (Sweigart, 2025).

The first section describes the value and where it comes from, with print as the standard example. The second section explains the test that decides whether a value is None, which uses the operator is instead of the equality sign.

There is exactly one None, which is what makes the identity test the right one. The expression None is None evaluates to True, type(None) reports NoneType, and bool(None) is False while None == False is also False, so None is neither true nor equal to the other values that count as false (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Because print gives back None, a line such as spam = print('hi') leaves spam bound to None, and that is usually how a learner meets the value without having gone looking for it.

nodes.label: None value
nodes.body: None is a value that represents the absence of a value. The textbook states that it is the only value of the NoneType data type, that other programming languages might call it null, nil or undefined, and that it must always be written with a capital N, just like the Booleans True and False (Sweigart, 2025). The library reference describes it as an object frequently used to represent the absence of a value, as when default arguments are not passed to a function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: None is a value that represents the absence of a value. The textbook states that it is the only value of the NoneType data type, that other programming languages might call it null, nil or undefined, and that it must always be written with a capital N, just like the Booleans True and False (Sweigart, 2025). The library reference describes it as an object frequently used to represent the absence of a value, as when default arguments are not passed to a function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

None is useful when a variable has to hold something that shouldn't be confused for a real value (Sweigart, 2025). A function that searches for a result can return None to mean that nothing was found, a parameter can use it as a default to mean that the caller gave no argument, and a variable can start as None until its real value is known.

The first place a learner meets it is the return value of print. After spam = print('Hello!'), the text Hello! is printed and spam holds None; printing spam then shows None, and the check None == spam gives True (Sweigart, 2025). The interpreter normally suppresses None when it would be the only value written, so a call to print typed into the interactive shell shows only its text (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The expression type(None).__name__ evaluates to 'NoneType', and the reference confirms that None is the sole instance of the NoneType type, that is, the only value of that type (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Because it is the only value of its type, any two Nones are the same object, which is the fact that the identity test of the next section relies on. None is also a keyword: keyword.iskeyword('None') is True, so a program that tries None = 3 stops with SyntaxError: cannot assign to None.

None is not zero, not an empty string and not False, even though a test in an if statement treats all of them as false. The reference lists the values interpreted as false as False, None, numeric zero of all types and empty strings and containers (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The difference matters when a function must tell a missing value from a real zero, as the next section shows.

nodes.definition: None is the only value of NoneType and stands for the absence of a value; print returns it, and PEP 8 says to compare with is.

nodes.label: Identity test
nodes.body: An identity test asks whether two names refer to the very same object. The operators is and is not perform it: the language reference says that x is y is true if and only if x and y are the same object (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The test is different from equality, which asks whether two values are equal in content.

paras.text: An identity test asks whether two names refer to the very same object. The operators is and is not perform it: the language reference says that x is y is true if and only if x and y are the same object (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The test is different from equality, which asks whether two values are equal in content.

For None the identity test is the correct and the safest question. The style guide states that comparisons to singletons like None should always be done with is or is not, never the equality operators (Van Rossum et al., 2001). Since there is exactly one None, saying that a name is None is the same as saying that it refers to that one object.

The textbook compares with equality, writing None == spam, which gives True and is not wrong in that example (Sweigart, 2025); the style guide asks that real programs use spam is None instead. The test appears in the default-argument pattern of this chapter, if L is None:, and in any function that must tell whether a caller supplied an argument.

The same value can be tested in two ways, and only one of them asks the right question. A function describe(x) that answers 'missing' if x is None else 'given' reports 'given' for the argument 0, since 0 is a real value. A careless version written as 'missing' if not x else 'given' reports 'missing' for both 0 and None, because the reference counts numeric zero as false as well (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The style guide warns of exactly this trap: beware of writing if x when you really mean if x is not None (Van Rossum et al., 2001). It also asks for is not instead of not ... is, which is easier to read. Do not use is to compare numbers or strings: it tests identity, not equality, and Python even warns when it is written with a literal number.

nodes.definition: The operators is and is not test whether two names refer to the very same object; PEP 8 says to compare with None this way.

nodes.label: Frames and the call stack
nodes.body: A frame is the record that Python keeps for one running function call, and the call stack is the pile of such records that exist at a given moment. The language reference explains that a code block is executed in an execution frame, which contains some administrative information and determines where and how execution continues after the block's execution has completed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter turns this machinery into a picture that a beginner can hold in mind.

paras.text: A frame is the record that Python keeps for one running function call, and the call stack is the pile of such records that exist at a given moment. The language reference explains that a code block is executed in an execution frame, which contains some administrative information and determines where and how execution continues after the block's execution has completed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter turns this machinery into a picture that a beginner can hold in mind.

Every call has to return to the place that made it, and a function may be called from many different places. Python can only manage this if it remembers, for each call that is still running, where to go back to. The frames and the stack are how it remembers, and they also explain two things that look unrelated: why each call has its own variables, and why an endless chain of calls ends with an error instead of running forever.

The textbook compares the call stack with a meandering conversation. You talk about Alice, are reminded of a story about Bob, and must first explain something about Carol; when the story about Carol ends you return to Bob and later to Alice. In a stack, items get added or removed from the top only, and the current topic is always at the top of the stack (Sweigart, 2025).

The branch has one group, the call stack, with four sections. The first gives the order in which calls start and return, the second names the frame object that records each call, the third shows how a program can look at the frames it is running inside, and the fourth treats recursion, in which a function calls itself and the stack grows deep.

The textbook itself says that the call stack is a technical detail that you don't strictly need to know about to write programs, and that it is enough to understand that function calls return to the line number they were called from (Sweigart, 2025). The reason to learn it anyway is that it makes the local and global scopes of the next branch easy to understand.

nodes.label: Call stack
nodes.body: The call stack is the stack of frames, one for each function call that has started and not yet returned. It is not a variable in the program; the textbook describes it as a section of your computer's memory that Python handles automatically behind the scenes (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The call stack is the stack of frames, one for each function call that has started and not yet returned. It is not a variable in the program; the textbook describes it as a section of your computer's memory that Python handles automatically behind the scenes (Sweigart, 2025).

The stack explains the order of the output of any program with nested calls, and it is the reason an error deep inside one function can be traced back through the functions that led to it. Every concept in this branch is a view of the same stack: its order, its records, the way a program can inspect it and the way it can overflow.

The sections of the branch take the stack in turn. They start with the order in which it grows and shrinks, continue with the frame object that is stored for each call, then show how to list the frames and how Python limits the depth, and finish with recursion.

The stack has a depth that can be read and reached. The call sys.getrecursionlimit() reports 1000 under the default settings, and a function that calls itself with no stopping condition ends with RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded, which is the stack refusing rather than the function's arithmetic failing (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The frames can be counted from inside a running program as well, with the inspect module, and that is how the sections below show the stack growing on each call and shrinking again on each return.

nodes.label: Call stack order
nodes.body: The call stack order is the order in which function calls start and finish when some of them call others. The textbook states the rule: calling a function doesn't send the execution on a one-way trip to the top of a function, because Python will remember which line of code called the function so that the execution can return there when it encounters a return statement (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The call stack order is the order in which function calls start and finish when some of them call others. The textbook states the rule: calling a function doesn't send the execution on a one-way trip to the top of a function, because Python will remember which line of code called the function so that the execution can return there when it encounters a return statement (Sweigart, 2025).

Without the stack, nested calls could not work. A function such as a() that calls b() must continue where it stopped once b() is done, and b() may in turn have called c() in the meantime. The stack keeps those waiting calls in the right order, with the function currently running at the top.

The textbook's program abcdCallStack.py defines four functions: a() calls b() and then d(), and b() calls c(). Running it prints eight lines in this order: a() starts, b() starts, c() starts, c() returns, b() returns, d() starts, d() returns and a() returns (Sweigart, 2025). The nesting of the output is the nesting of the calls: c() finishes first, although a() started first.

When the program calls a(), Python adds a frame for a at the top of the stack. The call to b() adds a frame above it, and the call to c() another one. When c() returns, its frame is removed from the top and execution continues in b() at the line after the call; the textbook stresses that frame objects always get added and removed from the top of the stack, and not from any other place (Sweigart, 2025). The top of the call stack is the currently executing function, and an empty call stack means that the execution is on a line outside all functions (Sweigart, 2025).

A function that returns does not skip the functions that are waiting below it. Execution comes back to the immediate caller, never directly to the first one, which is why the lines c() returns, b() returns and a() returns appear in that order and not at once.

nodes.definition: Python remembers which line called a function so that execution returns there, keeping the waiting calls on a stack of frames.

nodes.label: Frame object
nodes.body: A frame object is the record that Python creates for a function call and places on the call stack. The textbook says that frame objects store the line number of the original function call so that Python can remember where to return (Sweigart, 2025). The data model of the language describes frame objects as representing execution frames (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A frame object is the record that Python creates for a function call and places on the call stack. The textbook says that frame objects store the line number of the original function call so that Python can remember where to return (Sweigart, 2025). The data model of the language describes frame objects as representing execution frames (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Without a record of the caller, a function would have no way back. The frame is that record, and because each call gets its own frame, each call also gets its own set of local variables, which is how the same function can be running several times at once without the runs disturbing each other.

A program can look at its own frames with the inspect module. In a function show defined as f = inspect.currentframe() followed by return f.f_lineno, f.f_back.f_lineno, the first number is the line currently being executed in that function and the second is the line of the caller; for the example program they are 9 and 10, the second being the line that contains the call x = show(). The documentation describes f_lineno as the current line number in Python source code and f_back as the next outer frame, the frame's caller (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

When a function is called, Python creates a frame object on top of the call stack; when the call returns, it removes that frame object and moves the execution to the line number stored in it (Sweigart, 2025).
