The reference adds that a frame's f_back attribute points to the previous stack frame, towards the caller, or to None if this is the bottom stack frame (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the program in which inner() is called from outer(), the code name of the caller found through f_back is 'outer', and for a call made at the top level of the file it is '<module>'.

Frames belong to Python's internals. The documentation of the inspect module warns that keeping references to frame objects can make the objects they reach live much longer than expected, and advises removing the reference once the work with the frame is done (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Ordinary programs never need to touch a frame; it is a tool for debuggers and for understanding.

nodes.definition: The record Python creates for one call; it stores where the call came from, so execution can return there.

nodes.label: Stack inspection
nodes.body: Stack inspection means reading the call stack from within the program. The traceback module offers traceback.extract_stack(), which the documentation describes as extracting the raw traceback from the current stack frame (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The result is a list of entries, one per frame, each with the name of the function that frame belongs to.

paras.text: Stack inspection means reading the call stack from within the program. The traceback module offers traceback.extract_stack(), which the documentation describes as extracting the raw traceback from the current stack frame (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The result is a list of entries, one per frame, each with the name of the function that frame belongs to.

The stack is normally invisible, so being able to print it turns the textbook's picture into something a student can check. It is also how error reports are built: the lines of a traceback are the frames of the stack at the moment of the error, a point the exception section returns to.

In a program where a() returns b(), b() returns c(), and c() returns the names of the frames from traceback.extract_stack(), the list is ['<module>', 'a', 'b', 'c']. The bottom entry is the top level of the file, then each waiting function, and the last name is the function that asked: c, the top of the stack.

The interpreter also limits the depth of the stack. The documentation of sys.getrecursionlimit() calls the value the maximum depth of the Python interpreter stack and says that the limit prevents infinite recursion from causing an overflow of the C stack and crashing Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Under both Python 3.12 and 3.14 it is 1000, as the example evaluates.

A stack that grows past the limit does not crash the program silently; Python raises RecursionError. The exceptions documentation says that it is derived from RuntimeError and is raised when the interpreter detects that the maximum recursion depth is exceeded (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Derived from means that RecursionError is a more specific kind of RuntimeError, so a program prepared for the general kind is prepared for the specific one as well; the exceptions branch calls this relation a subclass. The limit is a safety net and not a number to rely on: code that needs more than a few hundred nested calls is usually better written with a loop.

nodes.definition: A program can list the frames it is running inside, and the interpreter stops a runaway chain of calls with a RecursionError.

nodes.label: Recursion
nodes.body: Recursion is the situation in which a function calls itself. The tutorial mentions it in passing: when a function calls another function, or calls itself recursively, a new local symbol table is created for that call (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Each call is therefore independent of the others, even though they all run the same body.

paras.text: Recursion is the situation in which a function calls itself. The tutorial mentions it in passing: when a function calls another function, or calls itself recursively, a new local symbol table is created for that call (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Each call is therefore independent of the others, even though they all run the same body.

Some problems are naturally defined in terms of smaller versions of themselves. The factorial of 5 is 5 times the factorial of 4, which is a definition that translates directly into a function that calls itself with a smaller number. Recursion is also the clearest way to see the call stack at work, because the stack gets as deep as the chain of calls.

For def factorial(n) that returns 1 when n <= 1 and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), the call factorial(5) gives 120 and factorial(10) gives 3628800. Five frames for factorial exist at the deepest moment of factorial(5), and they are removed one after another as the results are multiplied on the way back.

A recursive function needs a base case, a branch that returns without calling itself, so that the chain ends. The call stack holds one frame for each pending call, and each frame has its own value of n. When the deepest call returns 1, the frames below it are completed in reverse order, each multiplying its n by the value it receives.

A recursive function without a base case never ends. For def forever(): return forever(), the stack grows until Python stops it with RecursionError and the message maximum recursion depth exceeded; RecursionError is a subclass of RuntimeError. A base case that is never reached because the argument does not shrink has the same effect as having none.

nodes.definition: A function that calls itself; each call has its own frame, and a base case must end the chain or RecursionError follows.

nodes.label: Scope
nodes.body: A scope is the part of a program in which a name can be used, and the scope of a variable decides which variable a name refers to. The textbook asks the reader to think of a scope as a container for variables (Sweigart, 2025), and the language reference defines it as what determines the visibility of a name within a block (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This branch of the chapter explains the containers that exist, the rules that connect names with them, and the statements that bend the rules.

paras.text: A scope is the part of a program in which a name can be used, and the scope of a variable decides which variable a name refers to. The textbook asks the reader to think of a scope as a container for variables (Sweigart, 2025), and the language reference defines it as what determines the visibility of a name within a block (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This branch of the chapter explains the containers that exist, the rules that connect names with them, and the statements that bend the rules.

Scopes are what keep a large program understandable. The textbook explains that Python uses scoping because it enables a function to modify its variables, yet interact with the rest of the program through its parameters and its return value only, which narrows down the number of lines of code that might be causing a bug (Sweigart, 2025). A bad value in a local variable can be hunted inside one function; a bad value in a variable that every part of the program can change could have been set from anywhere.

Every program with a function has at least two scopes: the global scope that holds the names created outside all functions, and one local scope for each function call that is running. Beyond the textbook, a function defined inside another function has the outer function's scope around it, and every program can see the built-in names such as print and len.

The branch starts with the containers, which the reference calls namespaces: the local scope, the global scope, the enclosing scope of a nested function and the built-in scope. It continues with the rules that decide which of them a name belongs to: the four rules of the textbook, the lookup order behind them, the statements global and nonlocal, the symbol table that applies the rules before the program runs, and two error messages, NameError and UnboundLocalError.

The textbook allows global variables in small programs but calls it a bad habit to rely on them as programs get larger (Sweigart, 2025). The same habit is the main source of the surprising errors in this branch, because most of them happen when a function that reads a name is changed so that it also assigns it.

nodes.label: Namespaces
nodes.body: A namespace is the place where a variable is stored. The glossary adds that namespaces are implemented as dictionaries, which are tables that pair a name with a value, and that there are the local, global and built-in namespaces as well as nested namespaces in objects (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A scope is the region of the program from which a namespace is visible, and in everyday speech the two words are used for the same container.

paras.text: A namespace is the place where a variable is stored. The glossary adds that namespaces are implemented as dictionaries, which are tables that pair a name with a value, and that there are the local, global and built-in namespaces as well as nested namespaces in objects (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A scope is the region of the program from which a namespace is visible, and in everyday speech the two words are used for the same container.

Namespaces support modularity by preventing naming conflicts: the glossary's example is that the functions builtins.open and os.open() are distinguished by their namespaces (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The same idea lets two functions use the name eggs for different variables without disturbing each other.

The sections of this group describe the namespaces one by one: the local scope that every call creates, the single global scope, the scope of an enclosing function, the built-in scope, and the confusing but legal situation in which the same name is used in several of them.

The containers can be listed, which turns the rules into something a learner can watch. Inside a call the function locals() reports the names of that call alone while globals() reports the module's names, so a function whose only statement binds spam shows spam among its locals and not among the globals (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Two functions may each use the name eggs without disturbing each other, because every call makes a new local namespace that is discarded when the call returns.

nodes.label: Local scope
nodes.body: The local scope of a function call is the container for the parameters and for the variables assigned in the function while it runs. The textbook says that only code within a called function can access the parameters and variables assigned in that function, and that such a variable is called a local variable (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The local scope of a function call is the container for the parameters and for the variables assigned in the function while it runs. The textbook says that only code within a called function can access the parameters and variables assigned in that function, and that such a variable is called a local variable (Sweigart, 2025).

A local scope gives each call its own workspace. Because the workspace disappears afterwards, a function cannot leave clutter behind, and a variable called result in one function cannot be confused with a variable called result in another. This is the mechanism behind the textbook's image of a function as a black box.

In the program that defines spam with the line eggs = 'sss' and calls spam(), the variable eggs exists only while spam runs. The textbook explains that a new local scope gets created whenever a program calls a function, and that when the function returns the local scope gets destroyed, along with these variables (Sweigart, 2025).

The destruction has a visible effect. After the call, print(eggs) at the top level stops with NameError: name 'eggs' is not defined, because there is no variable of that name any more. A function that sets n = 0 and adds one to it always starts fresh: calling counter() twice gives 1 and 1, not 1 and 2, since the second call receives a new local scope in which n starts again.

Values that must survive from one call to the next cannot live in a local variable. They can be returned to the caller, which stores them, or they can live in a global variable, which brings the risks that the global scope section describes. The parameters of a function also belong to its local scope and are forgotten at the return.

nodes.definition: A variable assigned inside a function exists only in that call's local scope and is destroyed when the call returns.

nodes.label: Global scope
nodes.body: The global scope is the container for the variables assigned outside all functions. The textbook says that code anywhere in a program can access such variables, which are called global variables, and that a variable must be local or global; it cannot be both (Sweigart, 2025). The reference describes the same container as the namespace of the module that contains the code (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The global scope is the container for the variables assigned outside all functions. The textbook says that code anywhere in a program can access such variables, which are called global variables, and that a variable must be local or global; it cannot be both (Sweigart, 2025). The reference describes the same container as the namespace of the module that contains the code (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A global variable is the simplest way for different functions to share a value, which is why beginners reach for it first. It is also the reason the textbook recommends caution: when every function can change a variable, a bug caused by a bad value gives no hint about where the value was set.

The program that sets eggs = 'GLOBALGLOBAL' at the top level and then calls a function that prints eggs shows the usual use: the function does not assign the name, so it reads the global one and prints GLOBALGLOBAL.

There is only one global scope. It is created when the program begins and destroyed when the program terminates, at which time all its variables are forgotten, whereas a new local scope is created for every call (Sweigart, 2025). Code in a function can read a global variable freely; changing it needs the global statement that a later section describes.

The global scope is not the same as the built-in scope. A name such as print is found in neither the local nor the global scope of the program, and yet it works, because the built-in scope is searched last. Mixing the two up leads to the mistake of redefining a built-in name as a global variable.

nodes.definition: There is one global scope, created when the program begins and destroyed when it ends, and code in any function can read its variables.

nodes.label: Same-name variables
nodes.body: Variables with the same name can exist in different scopes at the same time, and they are different variables. The textbook states the fourth scope rule in these words: you can use the same name for different variables if they are in different scopes (Sweigart, 2025). A variable that hides another one of the same name in an outer scope is said to shadow it.

paras.text: Variables with the same name can exist in different scopes at the same time, and they are different variables. The textbook states the fourth scope rule in these words: you can use the same name for different variables if they are in different scopes (Sweigart, 2025). A variable that hides another one of the same name in an outer scope is said to shadow it.

The rule is what makes functions independent. A programmer writing spam does not need to know whether bacon already uses the name eggs. The cost is that a reader can be confused about which eggs is meant at a given line, which the FAQ describes by saying that an assignment to a variable in a scope makes it local to that scope and shadows any similarly named variable in the outer scope (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The textbook's program localGlobalSameName.py defines spam with its own eggs set to 'spam local', and bacon with another eggs set to 'bacon local' that calls spam and prints its own eggs again; at the top level eggs is 'global'. Calling bacon() and then printing eggs gives four lines: bacon local, spam local, bacon local and global (Sweigart, 2025).

The program contains three different variables that are all named eggs: one in the local scope of spam, one in the local scope of bacon, and one in the global scope (Sweigart, 2025). While spam runs, the eggs of bacon still exists, waiting on the call stack, and it has not been changed. When bacon prints eggs for the second time it still shows its own value.

Legal does not mean advisable. The textbook's advice is that, to simplify your life, you should avoid using the same name in different scopes and give all variables unique names, even when they appear in different scopes (Sweigart, 2025). In practice, this means that a function should not reuse the name of a global variable for something else.

nodes.definition: The same name in different scopes gives different variables; the book advises unique names to keep track of them.

nodes.label: Enclosing scope
nodes.body: An enclosing scope is the local scope of the function inside which another function is defined. The glossary calls the ability to refer to a variable in an enclosing definition a nested scope, and gives the example of a function defined inside another function referring to variables in the outer function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An enclosing scope is the local scope of the function inside which another function is defined. The glossary calls the ability to refer to a variable in an enclosing definition a nested scope, and gives the example of a function defined inside another function referring to variables in the outer function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The enclosing scope completes the picture of where a name can be found. A name used inside a nested function is searched in its own local scope first, then in the enclosing scopes from the nearest to the farthest, then in the global scope, and finally in the built-in scope, as the tutorial describes (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the program in which outer sets n = 21 and defines an inner function that returns n * 2, the call outer() evaluates to 42: the inner function has no n of its own and finds the one in outer. The worked example of this concept builds the same structure from two lambda expressions and evaluates to 42.

The glossary notes that nested scopes by default work only for reference and not for assignment: local variables both read and write in the innermost scope, and the nonlocal statement allows writing to outer scopes (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In other words, an inner function reads the variables of its enclosing function freely, but an assignment inside it creates a new local variable.

A name read from an enclosing scope is looked up when the inner function runs, not when it is defined. If the outer variable changes in between, the inner function sees the new value. The FAQ shows the surprising consequence for functions created in a loop, which all see the final value of the loop variable (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: The local scope of the function around a nested function; the inner function can read its variables.

nodes.label: Built-in scope
nodes.body: The built-in scope is the namespace that holds the names Python provides in every program, such as print, input, len and int. The language reference calls it the builtins namespace, the namespace of the module builtins, and says that names are resolved by searching the global namespace first and the builtins namespace next (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The built-in scope is the namespace that holds the names Python provides in every program, such as print, input, len and int. The language reference calls it the builtins namespace, the namespace of the module builtins, and says that names are resolved by searching the global namespace first and the builtins namespace next (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

This is why print works without any definition and without an import, even though the program never created that name. It is also why the FAQ can say that if global were required for all global references, you would have to declare as global every reference to a built-in function or to a component of an imported module (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The tutorial puts the built-ins at the end of the lookup order: variable references first look in the local symbol table, then in the local symbol tables of enclosing functions, then in the global symbol table, and finally in the table of built-in names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The check builtins.len is len evaluates to True, which shows that the len that a program sees is the one in the builtins module.

A function such as reads_len that returns len('abc') finds len in none of the scopes it owns, so the search ends in the built-in scope and the call evaluates to 3. A name assigned in a nearer scope hides the built-in one: inside a function, len = 3 makes len a local variable that equals 3, and the real len is untouched for the rest of the program.

Hiding a built-in name at the top level breaks every later use of it. After len = 3 at the top level of a program, the call len('abc') stops with TypeError: 'int' object is not callable, since the name now refers to the number 3. Avoid using built-in names such as len, print, max or type for variables.

nodes.definition: The scope searched last for a name; it holds print, len and the other built-in functions, which is why they work without being defined.

nodes.label: Scope rules
nodes.body: The scope rules are the statements that decide whether a name in a function is local or global, and what happens when a program breaks them. The textbook states two sets of rules: four rules that say what code can use which variables, and four rules for identifying whether a variable belongs to a local or the global scope (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The scope rules are the statements that decide whether a name in a function is local or global, and what happens when a program breaks them. The textbook states two sets of rules: four rules that say what code can use which variables, and four rules for identifying whether a variable belongs to a local or the global scope (Sweigart, 2025).

Following the rules is the difference between a program that works and one that stops with an error that looks arbitrary. The rules also explain a surprising fact: whether a name is local is decided from the text of the whole function, not from the line that is running.

The sections cover what code can reach which scope, the lookup order behind it, the two statements that change the rules, the table in which the compiler, the part of Python that translates the program into bytecode, records its decisions, and the two errors that appear when a name cannot be found. A last section covers the statement nonlocal, which the textbook omits.

The surprising rule can be shown in four lines. A function that prints eggs and later assigns to eggs makes eggs local for the whole of its body, so the print raises UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'eggs' where it is not associated with a value, even while a global eggs holds a perfectly good value (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Writing global eggs as the function's first statement removes the error and makes the assignment change the module's own variable, and nonlocal does the same for a name that belongs to an enclosing function.

nodes.label: Local isolation
nodes.body: Local isolation is the pair of rules that keeps the local variables of a function private. The textbook states them as: code that is in the global scope, outside all functions, can't use local variables; and code that is in one function's local scope can't use variables in any other local scope (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Local isolation is the pair of rules that keeps the local variables of a function private. The textbook states them as: code that is in the global scope, outside all functions, can't use local variables; and code that is in one function's local scope can't use variables in any other local scope (Sweigart, 2025).
Isolation is what makes a function a black box. A function can be rewritten, renamed or have its variables changed without affecting any other part of the program, because no other part can see them.

In the first case a function spam assigns eggs = 'sss', and the line print(eggs) after the call stops with NameError: name 'eggs' is not defined. In the second case spam sets eggs to 'SPAMSPAM' and calls bacon, which sets its own eggs to 'BACONBACON' and a variable ham; back in spam, print(eggs) shows SPAMSPAM, because bacon's variables are in another scope (Sweigart, 2025).

Python creates a new local scope whenever a program calls a function, even when the function is called from another function, and multiple local scopes can exist at the same time (Sweigart, 2025). The variable ham of bacon exists only during that call. If a third function tries to print ham, it stops with NameError: name 'ham' is not defined.

The only legitimate ways to move information between functions are the parameters and the return value. A learner who wants to read another function's variable should return it from that function, or pass it as an argument, and not reach for a global.

nodes.definition: Code in the global scope cannot use a local variable, and one function's local scope cannot use variables in another local scope.

nodes.label: Global access
nodes.body: Global access is the rule that code in a local scope can read global variables. The textbook gives the condition: because the function has no parameter with that name, nor any code that assigns the name a value, Python considers the function's use of the name to be a reference to the global variable (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Global access is the rule that code in a local scope can read global variables. The textbook gives the condition: because the function has no parameter with that name, nor any code that assigns the name a value, Python considers the function's use of the name to be a reference to the global variable (Sweigart, 2025).

Without this rule every function would need to be handed every constant, setting and helper function as a parameter. The FAQ gives the reason that the default is the way it is: if global were required for all global references, you'd be using global all the time (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the program where eggs = 'GLOBALGLOBAL' is assigned at the top level and spam only prints eggs, the call spam() prints GLOBALGLOBAL. The practice questions of the chapter use the same rule: a program assigns random_number = random.randint(1, 6) once at the top level and defines a function that only returns random_number (Sweigart, 2025).

That function returns the same number on every call, because the random choice was made once, when the global variable was assigned, and the function only reads it. Counting the different values among four calls gives 1. Calling randint inside the function would have chosen a new number each time.

Reading a global is allowed, but the first assignment inside the function changes the meaning of every use in that function. The FAQ states the rule briefly: variables that are only referenced inside a function are implicitly global, and if a variable is assigned a value anywhere within the function's body, it's assumed to be a local unless explicitly declared as global (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.example: print(eggs) inside spam() with no eggs of its own
nodes.definition: Code in a local scope can read global variables when it has no local variable of that name.

nodes.label: Name resolution
nodes.body: Name resolution is the process by which Python decides which variable a name refers to. The language reference states it in one sentence: when a name is used in a code block, it is resolved using the nearest enclosing scope (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook's four rules for scopes are the special cases of this one rule.

paras.text: Name resolution is the process by which Python decides which variable a name refers to. The language reference states it in one sentence: when a name is used in a code block, it is resolved using the nearest enclosing scope (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook's four rules for scopes are the special cases of this one rule.

A single rule is easier to remember and to apply than a list of exceptions. Once the order is known, every scope question can be answered by walking through the scopes from the nearest outward and stopping at the first one that has the name.

The tutorial gives the order: first the local symbol table, then the symbol tables of enclosing functions, then the global symbol table, and finally the table of built-in names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the program with a global x set to 'global', an outer function that sets x = 'enclosing', and an inner function that only returns x, the inner function returns 'enclosing', a second inner function that assigns x = 'local' returns 'local', and the global x is still 'global'.

The search finds the name in the nearest scope that has it and stops there. If the name is not found in any scope, the reference says that a NameError exception is raised (Python Software Foundation, 2026). If the name was bound in the current function but not yet given a value at the moment of use, an UnboundLocalError is raised instead, which is the subject of a later section.

Resolution depends on the structure of the program text, not on the order in which lines happen to run. A name is resolved in the local scope if the function assigns it anywhere, even in a branch that never executes, and then it is a local variable for the whole function, as the section on the symbol table shows.

nodes.definition: The lookup rule behind the scope rules: a name is resolved in the nearest enclosing scope, in the order local, enclosing, global, built-in.

nodes.label: NameError
nodes.body: NameError is the exception that Python raises when a name is used and no scope contains it. The library reference describes it as raised when a local or global name is not found, and states that the associated value is an error message that includes the name that could not be found (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: NameError is the exception that Python raises when a name is used and no scope contains it. The library reference describes it as raised when a local or global name is not found, and states that the associated value is an error message that includes the name that could not be found (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

It is the commonest error in beginners' programs and the one that the scope rules most directly explain. Reading the message correctly, a learner can tell at once whether the name was misspelled, used before it was created, or created in a scope that the line cannot see.

The chapter shows it in the first scope rule: print(eggs) at the top level, after a function has assigned eggs locally, gives NameError: name 'eggs' is not defined. A misspelled or differently capitalised name behaves the same way, since Python distinguishes capitals: after def Hello(), the call hello() reports that the name hello is not defined, and recent releases add the hint Did you mean: 'Hello'?

The reference says that when a name is not found at all, a NameError exception is raised (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Several of the situations in this chapter reach it by different roads: a call before the def statement has run, a variable that exists only in another function, a parameter used after its call has returned, and a function name that is only defined inside another function.

UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError, so an except clause for NameError also catches it. The two should not be confused when reading a message: NameError says there is no such name at all, while UnboundLocalError says that the name exists in the function but has no value yet.

nodes.definition: The error raised when a name is not found in any scope; its message includes the name, as in name 'eggs' is not defined.

nodes.label: Global statement
nodes.body: The global statement tells Python that a name inside a function refers to the global variable. The textbook explains that a line such as global eggs at the top of a function tells Python: in this function, eggs refers to the global variable, so don't create a local variable with this name (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference defines it as causing the listed identifiers to be interpreted as globals (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The global statement tells Python that a name inside a function refers to the global variable. The textbook explains that a line such as global eggs at the top of a function tells Python: in this function, eggs refers to the global variable, so don't create a local variable with this name (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference defines it as causing the listed identifiers to be interpreted as globals (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Reading a global needs no declaration, but changing one does: the reference notes that it would be impossible to assign to a global variable without global (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The requirement is deliberate, since the FAQ says that requiring global for assigned variables provides a bar against unintended side-effects (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the textbook's globalStatement.py, the function spam declares global eggs and then assigns eggs = 'spam'. After the top-level eggs was set to 'global', calling spam() and printing eggs gives spam, because no local eggs is ever created (Sweigart, 2025).

The statement applies to the entire current scope, and a SyntaxError is raised if the variable is used or assigned to before its global declaration in that scope (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that assigns eggs = 1 and only afterwards declares global eggs is rejected with SyntaxError: name 'eggs' is assigned to before global declaration, before the program runs.

Needing global is a hint that the design may be wrong. The textbook says that writing functions without global variables is encouraged, which makes it possible to treat each function as a black box (Sweigart, 2025). Pass values in as parameters and take results out as return values, and keep the global statement for the few cases that truly need it.

nodes.definition: A global statement makes a name in the function refer to the global variable, so assigning to it changes the global.

nodes.label: Scope identification
nodes.body: Scope identification is the set of four rules with which the textbook decides whether a variable belongs to a local scope or the global scope. A variable in the global scope, outside all functions, is always a global variable; a variable in a function with a global statement is a global variable in that function; otherwise, if a function uses a variable in an assignment statement, it is a local variable; however, if the function uses a variable but never in an assignment statement, it is a global variable (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Scope identification is the set of four rules with which the textbook decides whether a variable belongs to a local scope or the global scope. A variable in the global scope, outside all functions, is always a global variable; a variable in a function with a global statement is a global variable in that function; otherwise, if a function uses a variable in an assignment statement, it is a local variable; however, if the function uses a variable but never in an assignment statement, it is a global variable (Sweigart, 2025).

The four rules turn the earlier discussion into a procedure that a student can carry out on paper. Looking at a function, one finds first any global statement, then any assignment, and the name is classified accordingly. The rules also fit into the one lookup rule of the previous section.

The textbook's sameNameLocalGlobal.py has three functions that use the name eggs. In spam, which declares global eggs, it is the global variable; in bacon, which assigns eggs = 'bacon', it is local; and in ham, which only prints eggs, it is the global variable (Sweigart, 2025). Running spam(), printing eggs, then running bacon() and printing eggs, then ham() prints spam three times, because only spam changes the global.

The decision does not depend on the order of the lines. The reference explains that the local variables of a code block can be determined by scanning the entire text of the block for name binding operations (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and the symbol table of the next but one section shows the result: the same name eggs is global in spam, local in bacon and global in ham.

Rule 4 has a trap that rule 3 creates: a function that only uses a name is reading the global one, but adding one assignment anywhere in the function turns every use of that name in it into the local variable. This is the origin of the error described in the section on UnboundLocalError.

nodes.definition: A name is global if used outside all functions or declared global, local if the function assigns it, and global if the function only reads it.

nodes.label: Symbol table
nodes.body: A symbol table is the table in which the Python compiler records every name used in a block and what kind of name it is. The documentation of the symtable module says that symbol tables are generated by the compiler from the syntax tree, the structured form of the program text, just before bytecode is generated, and that the symbol table is responsible for calculating the scope of every identifier in the code (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial uses the same term: the execution of a function introduces a new symbol table used for the local variables of the function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A symbol table is the table in which the Python compiler records every name used in a block and what kind of name it is. The documentation of the symtable module says that symbol tables are generated by the compiler from the syntax tree, the structured form of the program text, just before bytecode is generated, and that the symbol table is responsible for calculating the scope of every identifier in the code (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial uses the same term: the execution of a function introduces a new symbol table used for the local variables of the function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The table explains why the scope rules look at the text of a function and not at what is executed. Python decides which names are local before the first line of the function runs, so no behaviour at run time can change the decision.

The module symtable lets a program read the compiler's decisions. For a source with spam declaring global eggs, bacon assigning eggs and ham only printing it, the table lists eggs as global for spam, local for bacon and global for ham, which agrees with the textbook's four rules.

The decision is made for the whole function body at once. In a function that contains if False: followed by an indented assignment x = 'local', and then returns x, the assignment never runs, and yet x is a local variable of the function, so the call stops with UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'x' where it is not associated with a value. The global x that was set earlier is not used.

The symbol table is an inspection tool and not part of normal programming. Its structure can change between releases: in Python 3.14 every function in this example also has a separate block for its annotations, which the example filters out by name. Rely on the rules of the language, not on the layout of the table.

nodes.definition: The compiler's table recording whether each name in a block is local or global, built before the program runs; the symtable module can show it.

nodes.label: UnboundLocalError
nodes.body: UnboundLocalError is the exception raised when a function uses a local variable before any value has been assigned to it. The library reference describes it as raised when a reference is made to a local variable in a function or method, but no value has been bound to that variable, and states that it is a subclass of NameError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook explains the name: in Python, binding is another way of saying assigning (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: UnboundLocalError is the exception raised when a function uses a local variable before any value has been assigned to it. The library reference describes it as raised when a reference is made to a local variable in a function or method, but no value has been bound to that variable, and states that it is a subclass of NameError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook explains the name: in Python, binding is another way of saying assigning (Sweigart, 2025).

The error is confusing because the name does exist in the program: a global variable of the same name was perhaps assigned earlier. It appears exactly when the rule of scope identification and the order of the lines disagree, and understanding it is the best test of whether a learner has understood how Python classifies names.

The textbook's sameNameError.py prints eggs on its first line and assigns eggs = 'spam local' on its second, while a global eggs exists. Python sees the assignment and therefore considers any mention of eggs in spam to be a local variable; because print(eggs) runs first, the local variable does not exist yet, and Python won't fall back to using the global eggs (Sweigart, 2025).

The FAQ gives a second form of the same mistake: with a global x = 10, a function that prints x and then executes x += 1 fails, because the assignment x += 1 makes x local (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Declaring global x repairs it when the global is meant, as does a nonlocal declaration for the variable of an enclosing function; renaming the local variable repairs it when it is not.

The wording of the message has changed. The textbook prints local variable 'eggs' referenced before assignment, which is what Python 3.10 prints for the program, but Python 3.11 and every later release, including 3.12 and 3.14, print cannot access local variable 'eggs' where it is not associated with a value. The kind of error, which Python calls its class, and the cause are the same, so a program must match the class and never the message.

nodes.definition: Using a local variable before it is assigned raises UnboundLocalError; since Python 3.11 the message reads cannot access local variable where it is not associated with a value.

nodes.label: Nonlocal statement
nodes.body: The nonlocal statement lets a nested function assign to a variable of the function around it. The language reference says that it causes the listed identifiers to refer to names previously bound in nonlocal scopes, which are the local scopes of the enclosing functions, and that it allows encapsulated code to rebind such nonlocal identifiers (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook does not cover it.

paras.text: The nonlocal statement lets a nested function assign to a variable of the function around it. The language reference says that it causes the listed identifiers to refer to names previously bound in nonlocal scopes, which are the local scopes of the enclosing functions, and that it allows encapsulated code to rebind such nonlocal identifiers (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook does not cover it.

It completes the set of choices for where an assignment goes. An assignment inside a function normally creates a local variable, global makes it go to the module's variable, and nonlocal makes it go to the nearest enclosing function's variable. PEP 3104 gives the historical reason: before it, Python code could refer to a name in any enclosing scope, but could only rebind names in two scopes, the local scope and the module-global scope (Yee, 2006).

In outer, set n = 0 and define inner with the line nonlocal n and the statement n += 1. After outer calls inner twice and returns n, it returns 2. Without the nonlocal line, the statement n += 1 would make n a local variable of inner, which has no value yet, and the call stops with UnboundLocalError.

If a name is bound in more than one nonlocal scope, the nearest binding is used (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The statement applies to the entire scope of the function and must come before any use of the name there. If the name is not bound in any enclosing function, the program is rejected before it runs with SyntaxError: no binding for nonlocal 'q' found.

Do not use nonlocal when a return value would do. Like global, it makes a function depend on state outside itself, and a reader has to look at the enclosing function to understand it. It is useful mainly for small helper functions that keep a counter or a running total for their enclosing function.

nodes.definition: A nonlocal statement lets an inner function rebind a name of the enclosing function, between the local and the global case.

nodes.label: Error handling
nodes.body: Error handling is the part of a program that decides what happens when something goes wrong. In Python an error that stops a statement is called an exception, and the language has two statements for dealing with it: try marks the code that might fail, and except says what to do when it does. The textbook puts the problem plainly: right now, getting an error, or exception, in a Python program means the entire program will crash (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Error handling is the part of a program that decides what happens when something goes wrong. In Python an error that stops a statement is called an exception, and the language has two statements for dealing with it: try marks the code that might fail, and except says what to do when it does. The textbook puts the problem plainly: right now, getting an error, or exception, in a Python program means the entire program will crash (Sweigart, 2025).

A program that crashes on the first unexpected input cannot be used for real work. The textbook says that in real-world programs you want the program to detect errors, handle them, and then continue to run (Sweigart, 2025), and its chapter summary adds that the try and except statements make programs more resilient to common error cases. A program that handles an error can also give a useful message, such as asking the user to type a number again, where an unhandled error shows a traceback that only a programmer can read.

The branch has one group, Exceptions. It begins with the try and except statements themselves, follows an error out of a function into the code that called it, and covers the newest change to the except line. It then looks at the objects that carry an error, the report Python prints when nobody handles one, the divide-by-zero error that the chapter uses as its example, and the family tree that decides which except clause catches which error.

When a statement raises an exception, Python stops running the block it is in and looks for a handler: an except clause, on a try statement, that names a matching exception. If one is found its block runs and the program continues after the try statement. If none is found anywhere in the chain of calls, the program ends with a traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The textbook points out that most of the time exceptions indicate a bug in your code that you need to fix (Sweigart, 2025). Handling an error is the right tool for failures that can be expected and recovered from, such as a missing file or text that is not a number, and the wrong tool for hiding a mistake in the program itself.

nodes.label: Exceptions
nodes.body: An exception is Python's way of reporting that a statement could not be carried out. The tutorial separates two kinds of mistake: syntax errors, also known as parsing errors, and errors detected during execution, which are called exceptions and are not unconditionally fatal (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This group is about the second kind, and about the statements that let a program survive them.

paras.text: An exception is Python's way of reporting that a statement could not be carried out. The tutorial separates two kinds of mistake: syntax errors, also known as parsing errors, and errors detected during execution, which are called exceptions and are not unconditionally fatal (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This group is about the second kind, and about the statements that let a program survive them.

The tutorial notes that most exceptions are not handled by programs, however, and result in error messages (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Knowing how an exception travels, what it carries and which handler catches it turns those messages from a source of panic into a description of what happened, and lets a program choose to recover when recovery makes sense.

The sections follow the life of one exception: the statements that catch it, the way it leaves a function, the spelling for catching several kinds at once, the object that Python creates for it, the report printed when it is not caught, the arithmetic error used as the chapter's example, and the hierarchy of classes that organises all of them.

Two rules govern where an exception can be caught, and a program may rely on both. A handler catches an exception raised anywhere inside the call it guards, however deep, so a try statement around a call catches a ZeroDivisionError raised in that call's own body. A handler for a class catches every subclass of it as well, so except Exception catches ZeroDivisionError, whose own chain of classes runs ZeroDivisionError, ArithmeticError, Exception, BaseException (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Several kinds are caught at once by naming them in a tuple, and the first matching except clause of a try statement is the one that runs.

nodes.label: Try and except
nodes.body: A try statement has two parts. The code that could potentially have an error is put in a try clause, and the program execution moves to the start of a following except clause if an error happens (Sweigart, 2025). The except line names the kind of error it handles, and the block under it holds the code that deals with that error.

paras.text: A try statement has two parts. The code that could potentially have an error is put in a try clause, and the program execution moves to the start of a following except clause if an error happens (Sweigart, 2025). The except line names the kind of error it handles, and the block under it holds the code that deals with that error.

Without a handler, the first error ends the program. With one, the program can report a problem in its own words and go on with its work. The textbook motivates this with a later chapter, in which a missing file raises FileNotFoundError and the program may ask the user for the filename again rather than crash (Sweigart, 2025).

The textbook puts the divide-by-zero code of its function spam inside a try clause, with the line except ZeroDivisionError: below it. Called with 2, 12, 0 and 1, the program prints 21.0, then 3.5, then Error: Invalid argument., then None, then 42.0. The None comes from the third call, because the handler prints a message but the function then ends without a return statement and supplies None, which print shows.

The tutorial gives the rules. First the try clause is executed. If no exception occurs the except clause is skipped. If an exception occurs, the rest of the try clause is skipped, and if its type matches the exception named after the except keyword, the except clause is executed and execution continues after the try and except block. If the type does not match, the exception is passed on to outer try statements, and if no handler is found, it is an unhandled exception and execution stops with an error message (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

An exception that does not match is not swallowed. When spam is called with the text 'a' instead of a number, the division raises a TypeError, which the clause for ZeroDivisionError does not match, and the program ends with the message unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'int' and 'str'. The tutorial adds that a handler only handles exceptions that occur in the corresponding try clause, not in other handlers of the same try statement (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: Code in a try clause that raises an error jumps to the matching except clause, and execution continues after the try statement.

nodes.label: Error in a called function
nodes.body: A try clause also catches the errors of the functions it calls. The textbook says that any errors that occur in function calls in a try block will also be caught (Sweigart, 2025), so the try statement does not have to be in the same function as the statement that fails.

paras.text: A try clause also catches the errors of the functions it calls. The textbook says that any errors that occur in function calls in a try block will also be caught (Sweigart, 2025), so the try statement does not have to be in the same function as the statement that fails.

This lets one handler protect many calls, and it keeps the error handling in the place where the program knows what to do about the error. A function such as spam can stay short and simply fail; the code that called it decides whether failure means a message, a second attempt or a clean exit.

In the textbook's second version of the divide-by-zero program, spam only divides, and the four print(spam(...)) lines are inside the try clause. The output is 21.0, then 3.5, then Error: Invalid argument. The fourth call, print(spam(1)), is never executed.

The textbook explains why: once the execution jumps to the code in the except clause, it does not return to the try clause, but continues moving down the program as normal (Sweigart, 2025). The error leaves spam and passes to the code that called it. The traceback of the unhandled version shows the two frames the error passed through, the line in the main program that called spam and the line inside spam that divided; the handler of the second version belongs to the first of them, the main program.

Where the try statement is placed decides how much code is skipped. With the try inside spam, as in the first version, the failing call returns None and the program goes on to the fourth call, so 42.0 is printed. With the try around all four calls, the program skips the fourth call as well. Neither placement is wrong; they answer different questions, which are whether each call is allowed to fail alone and whether the first failure ends the whole group of calls.

nodes.definition: An error raised inside a function called from a try clause is caught by that clause, and execution does not return into the try clause.

nodes.label: Several exception types in one except
nodes.body: One except clause can name several exception types, so that the same block of code handles any of them. The tutorial's try statement says that an except clause may name multiple exceptions and shows the form except RuntimeError, TypeError, NameError: with no brackets around the names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That form is new in Python 3.14, and the older form, which puts the names in brackets, separated by commas, still works.

paras.text: One except clause can name several exception types, so that the same block of code handles any of them. The tutorial's try statement says that an except clause may name multiple exceptions and shows the form except RuntimeError, TypeError, NameError: with no brackets around the names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That form is new in Python 3.14, and the older form, which puts the names in brackets, separated by commas, still works.

The change comes from PEP 758, whose abstract says that it allows unparenthesized except and except* blocks only when not using the as clause. Its authors call the brackets a Python 2 remnant and argue that dropping them makes the syntax more consistent with other parts of the language where parentheses are optional (Galindo Salgado and Cannon, 2024).

Take a function that divides 10 by int(x) and should answer bad for both a zero and a text that is not a number. The call with '2' gives 5.0, and the calls with '0' and 'puppy' each give bad. With the names in brackets the function works in Python 3.12 and 3.14. Written as except ZeroDivisionError, ValueError: it gives the same results in Python 3.14, while Python 3.12 refuses to run the program and reports SyntaxError: multiple exception types must be parenthesized.

The semantics are unchanged: the interpreter will catch any of the listed exceptions, whether or not they are in brackets (Galindo Salgado and Cannon, 2024). A separate except clause for each type is the other choice, and it is the right one when the types need different responses. With one clause for ZeroDivisionError returning zero and one for ValueError returning not a number, the same three calls give 5.0, zero and not a number. The tutorial notes that a try statement may have more than one except clause and at most one handler will be executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Brackets are still required with the as clause. In Python 3.14 the line except ZeroDivisionError, ValueError as e: is a syntax error with the message multiple exception types must be parenthesized when using 'as'. PEP 758 also warns that in Python 2 the unparenthesized form meant something else, with the first name as the exception type and the second as the variable that receives the exception. The new form does not reintroduce that meaning (Galindo Salgado and Cannon, 2024). A program that must run on a release before 3.14 should keep the brackets.

nodes.definition: Since Python 3.14 an except clause can list several exception types without brackets when it has no as clause.

nodes.label: Exception object
nodes.body: An exception is an object. The tutorial explains that when an exception occurs it may have associated values, also known as the exception's arguments, and that an except clause may specify a variable after the exception name; the variable is bound to the exception instance, the object created for this occurrence of the error, which typically has an args attribute that stores the arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An attribute here is a named piece of data that belongs to an object and is reached with a dot.

paras.text: An exception is an object. The tutorial explains that when an exception occurs it may have associated values, also known as the exception's arguments, and that an except clause may specify a variable after the exception name; the variable is bound to the exception instance, the object created for this occurrence of the error, which typically has an args attribute that stores the arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An attribute here is a named piece of data that belongs to an object and is reached with a dot.

Catching an error is often not enough, since the program or its user also wants to know what went wrong. The object carries that information: its type says what kind of failure it was, and its arguments hold the details, usually a message in words. A program can print the message, write it to a file or look at its parts, which the textbook's examples do not do.

For try: 1 / 0 followed by except ZeroDivisionError as e:, the type's name is ZeroDivisionError, the text of e is division by zero, and e.args is ('division by zero',), a tuple, which is a fixed group of values written in brackets. The same pattern with int('puppy') gives a ValueError whose text is invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'puppy'.

The tutorial notes that built-in exception types define __str__() to print all the arguments without explicitly accessing .args (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That is why print(e) shows the message alone. The library reference describes args as the tuple of arguments given when the exception object is created, and says that some built-in exceptions expect a certain number of arguments while others are usually called only with a single string giving an error message (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The name after as does not survive the except clause. The reference says that when an exception has been assigned using as target, it is cleared at the end of the except clause, so the exception must be assigned to a different name to be able to refer to it after the clause (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that prints e after the clause fails with NameError: name 'e' is not defined, while a program that first stores e in another name, as in saved = e, can still read saved.args.

nodes.definition: Python creates an object for every exception; as binds it to a name, and its args and its text describe what went wrong.

nodes.label: Traceback
nodes.body: A traceback is the report that Python prints when an exception is not handled. The tutorial describes its two parts: the last line indicates what happened, naming the exception type and giving detail, and the preceding part shows the context where the exception occurred, in the form of a stack traceback listing source lines (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A traceback is the report that Python prints when an exception is not handled. The tutorial describes its two parts: the last line indicates what happened, naming the exception type and giving detail, and the preceding part shows the context where the exception occurred, in the form of a stack traceback listing source lines (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The traceback is the first tool for finding a bug, because it says both what failed and where. The textbook uses it in just this way: from the line number given in the error message, you know that the return statement in spam() is causing the error (Sweigart, 2025). Reading it from the bottom up, first the message and then the lines above it, is quicker than reading the program from the top.

For the textbook's zeroDivide.py, the traceback has a first line, Traceback (most recent call last):, then one pair of lines for each call the error passed through, and last the line ZeroDivisionError: division by zero. Run as a program, the two calls it lists are the call print(spam(0)) at line 6 of the main program and the statement return 42 / divide_by at line 2 inside spam.

The traceback is the call stack written out. The call that was running when the error happened comes last, which is what the words most recent call last refer to. Each pair of lines names a file, a line number and the function in which the line sits, followed by the source line. The main program is shown as <module>. A program that ends this way also ends with exit status 1, the number that a program hands to the system when it ends, where zero means success.

The printed form is not identical between releases. The textbook's listing shows a Windows path, and your own file names will differ. The tutorial's examples also show marker lines under the source line, which the textbook's listing does not have, and the wording of some messages changed between 3.12 and 3.14, so a program should not compare the text of a traceback.

nodes.definition: The report Python prints when an exception is not handled: the lines of the calls it passed through, and last the exception's type and message.

nodes.label: ZeroDivisionError
nodes.body: ZeroDivisionError is the exception that Python raises when you divide by zero. The library reference describes it as raised when the second argument of a division or modulo operation is zero, and says the associated value is a string indicating the type of the operands and the operation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook introduces it in one sentence: a ZeroDivisionError happens whenever you try to divide a number by zero (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: ZeroDivisionError is the exception that Python raises when you divide by zero. The library reference describes it as raised when the second argument of a division or modulo operation is zero, and says the associated value is a string indicating the type of the operands and the operation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook introduces it in one sentence: a ZeroDivisionError happens whenever you try to divide a number by zero (Sweigart, 2025).

Division by zero has no answer, so the language cannot return a value, and the only honest choices are to stop or to hand the decision to the program. Making it an exception that can be caught lets the code that knows the meaning of the division decide what to do, as the chapter's function spam does with a message.

The chapter's function returns 42 / divide_by. Called with 2 it gives 21.0 and with 12 it gives 3.5, and with 0 it raises ZeroDivisionError: division by zero. The statements 1 // 0 and 1 % 0 raise the same exception, because floor division and modulo also have a second operand that must not be zero.

The check is made when the operation runs, not when the program is read, so a program that contains 42 / 0 starts normally and fails only when that line is reached. The exception object is created, the statement stops and the search for a handler begins, as for every exception. ZeroDivisionError is a subclass of ArithmeticError, so a handler written for ArithmeticError would catch it too.

The wording of the message depends on the release. In Python 3.14 the statements 1 / 0, 1 // 0 and 1 % 0 all end with division by zero. In Python 3.12 the same statements end with division by zero, integer division or modulo by zero, and integer modulo by zero. A program should catch the type of the exception, which is stable, and should not compare the text.

nodes.definition: The exception raised when the second operand of a division or a modulo operation is zero.

nodes.label: Exception hierarchy
nodes.body: The built-in exceptions are classes, kinds of object like the int and str of chapter 1, arranged in a tree, and the library reference lists the whole tree. An exception object is an instance of its class, the way the number 5 is an instance of int. A class that is lower in the tree is a subclass of the classes above it. ZeroDivisionError sits under ArithmeticError, which sits under Exception, which sits under BaseException (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The reference says that ArithmeticError is the base class for the built-in exceptions raised for various arithmetic errors, namely OverflowError, ZeroDivisionError and FloatingPointError.

paras.text: The built-in exceptions are classes, kinds of object like the int and str of chapter 1, arranged in a tree, and the library reference lists the whole tree. An exception object is an instance of its class, the way the number 5 is an instance of int. A class that is lower in the tree is a subclass of the classes above it. ZeroDivisionError sits under ArithmeticError, which sits under Exception, which sits under BaseException (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The reference says that ArithmeticError is the base class for the built-in exceptions raised for various arithmetic errors, namely OverflowError, ZeroDivisionError and FloatingPointError.

The tree decides which handler catches which error. The tutorial states the rule: a class in an except clause matches exceptions which are instances of the class itself or one of its derived classes, but not the other way around, so an except clause listing a derived class does not match instances of its base classes (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A programmer can therefore choose how wide a handler is, from one exact error to a whole family.

In the chapter, UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError and RecursionError is a subclass of RuntimeError, which is why a handler for NameError also catches a local variable used too early. A program that divides by zero inside try, and has except ArithmeticError, prints the type ZeroDivisionError for what it caught. A handler for KeyError does not catch it, and the error passes to the outer handler.

When an exception is raised, Python goes through the except clauses of the try statement from top to bottom, and the first matching clause is triggered (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A narrow class must therefore be written before a broad one, because a broad class written first matches everything below it. If a clause for ArithmeticError is written before a clause for ZeroDivisionError, the narrow clause never runs, because dividing by zero is already handled by the first. The tutorial shows the same effect with three classes: listed from the base class first, its example prints B three times instead of B, C, D.

Not every exception is under Exception. KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit are direct subclasses of BaseException, and the reference gives the reason: they inherit from BaseException so as not to be accidentally caught by code that catches Exception and thus prevent the interpreter from exiting (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler written for Exception is therefore the widest handler that is normally safe. The widest of all, for BaseException, would also stop a user from pressing Ctrl-C to end the program.

nodes.definition: Exception classes form a family tree, and an except clause catches the named class and all classes derived from it.

nodes.label: Short programs
nodes.body: This branch collects the programs that the chapter uses to put its ideas to work. Two of them are short animation programs, zigzag and spike, which print lines of characters until the user stops them. Two are practice programs, the Collatz sequence and input validation, which the textbook leaves to the reader. Each program is built from parts that have already been explained: functions, loops, string replication, try and except.

paras.text: This branch collects the programs that the chapter uses to put its ideas to work. Two of them are short animation programs, zigzag and spike, which print lines of characters until the user stops them. Two are practice programs, the Collatz sequence and input validation, which the textbook leaves to the reader. Each program is built from parts that have already been explained: functions, loops, string replication, try and except.

The textbook introduces the first program with the words that it will use the programming concepts you have learned so far to create a small animation program (Sweigart, 2025). Writing a whole program is the real test of understanding, because it shows whether the pieces fit together, which a single statement cannot show. The programs also bring in three small tools that the chapter has not met yet, the time.sleep function, the KeyboardInterrupt exception and the sys.exit function.

The branch has two groups. Animation covers zigzag and spike and the three tools they need. Practice programs covers the Collatz sequence and the extra step of making that program safe against wrong input.

Every program here has the same shape: an import line, a block of work that may repeat, and a try statement whose except clause deals with the one event that the program expects, the user pressing Ctrl-C. Reading them as variations of that shape makes each one shorter to understand.

The animation programs never end by themselves, so they cannot be run to completion in a test. The numbers quoted in this branch come from the same logic executed for a fixed number of steps, without the pause, and are labelled as such.

nodes.label: Animation programs
nodes.body: An animation program draws something new at regular intervals, so that the output seems to move. The textbook's two examples need no graphics: each prints a line of characters, waits one tenth of a second and prints the next, and the changing position or length of the lines makes a pattern that scrolls up the screen (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: An animation program draws something new at regular intervals, so that the output seems to move. The textbook's two examples need no graphics: each prints a line of characters, waits one tenth of a second and prints the next, and the changing position or length of the lines makes a pattern that scrolls up the screen (Sweigart, 2025).

These programs show a loop that does not stop, and the problem that follows from it: a program that never ends needs a way for the user to end it. The solution the textbook gives is the same in both programs, and it is the reason that this group also contains the sections on waiting, on interruption and on exiting.

The sections follow the order of the textbook: the zigzag program, the spike program, the time.sleep function both programs use for their pause, the KeyboardInterrupt exception that Ctrl-C raises, and the sys.exit function that the exception handler calls.

The pause and the stop can both be measured. Ten passes of a loop with time.sleep(0.1) in each take about one second together, and that is what makes the printed lines read as movement rather than as a wall of text (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The stop works because an interrupt from the keyboard raises KeyboardInterrupt, which inherits from BaseException rather than from Exception, so a handler written as except Exception does not catch it while a handler that names KeyboardInterrupt does, and that handler is what lets the program leave through sys.exit() instead of through a traceback.

nodes.label: Zigzag program
nodes.body: The zigzag program prints a band of eight asterisks over and over, moving it to the right until it is 20 spaces in, then back to the left, forever. The textbook says that the program creates a back-and-forth zigzag pattern until the user stops it (Sweigart, 2025). It keeps two variables: indent counts the spaces before the band, and indent_increasing holds a Boolean value that says whether the indentation is growing or shrinking.

paras.text: The zigzag program prints a band of eight asterisks over and over, moving it to the right until it is 20 spaces in, then back to the left, forever. The textbook says that the program creates a back-and-forth zigzag pattern until the user stops it (Sweigart, 2025). It keeps two variables: indent counts the spaces before the band, and indent_increasing holds a Boolean value that says whether the indentation is growing or shrinking.

The program shows how a few lines of state can produce a changing picture. Nothing in it is complicated, but it uses a main loop, a decision that changes direction at two limits, and string replication in one place, which makes it a good first program that combines the tools of the earlier chapters.
The first three lines it prints are the eight asterisks with no indent, one space and two spaces.

The main loop is while True. In each pass print(' ' * indent, end='') prints the spaces and, because end is an empty string, no newline, and then a second print prints the asterisks. If indent_increasing is true, indent grows by 1, and when it reaches 20 the flag is set to false; otherwise indent shrinks by 1, and when it reaches 0 the flag is set to true. Executed for 41 passes without the pause, and numbering the passes from 0, the indent is 0 in pass 0, 1 in pass 1, 19 in pass 19, 20 in pass 20, 19 in pass 21, 1 in pass 39 and 0 in pass 40. The largest value is 20, so one trip there and back takes 40 passes.

The program is wrapped in a try statement so that Ctrl-C can end it, which the sections on KeyboardInterrupt and sys.exit explain. Without the wrapper, the same keypress would end the program with a traceback. The upper limit, 20, is written into the program as a plain number, so changing how far the band travels means changing that number in the test.

nodes.definition: A loop that prints eight asterisks, indented by a number that grows to 20 and then shrinks to 0, again and again.

nodes.label: Spike program
nodes.body: The spike program draws a triangular spike of dashes that scrolls up the screen, forever. The textbook describes it as a program that uses string replication and nested loops to draw spikes (Sweigart, 2025). Its first for loop prints lines with increasing length and its second prints lines with decreasing length.

paras.text: The spike program draws a triangular spike of dashes that scrolls up the screen, forever. The textbook describes it as a program that uses string replication and nested loops to draw spikes (Sweigart, 2025). Its first for loop prints lines with increasing length and its second prints lines with decreasing length.

It is a short example of how the range function controls a loop. The two loops differ only in their range, and each print uses the same expression, '-' * (i * i), so the shape of the whole picture is decided by two lines of numbers.

The first loop uses range(1, 9), which gives 1 through 8, and the second uses range(7, 1, -1), which gives 7 down to 2. The lengths of the printed lines are therefore 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 49, 36, 25, 16, 9 and 4, which is fourteen lines for each trip through the main loop.

In each pass of a loop the variable i takes the next value from its range, and the string '-' is replicated i * i times. The textbook points out that the range of the second loop starts at 7, so the longest line, 64, is printed once, and that it counts down to 1, not including 1, so the shortest line of the second half is 4. The textbook also says that you can modify the 9 and the 7 values if you want to change how wide the spike becomes (Sweigart, 2025).

The textbook calls the lengths exponentially longer, but squares grow more slowly than that. The differences between neighbouring lengths in the first half are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15, which grow by a steady 2, a pattern of quadratic growth. Each trip through the main loop prints 8 lines from the first range and 6 from the second.

nodes.definition: Two for loops print lines of dashes whose lengths are the squares from 1 to 64 and back down to 4, again and again.

nodes.label: The time.sleep function
nodes.body: The function time.sleep pauses a program. The library reference says that it suspends execution of the calling thread for the given number of seconds, and that the argument may be a floating-point number to indicate a more precise sleep time (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook admits that it has not discussed the function yet and says that it introduces a one-tenth-of-a-second pause in the program (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The function time.sleep pauses a program. The library reference says that it suspends execution of the calling thread for the given number of seconds, and that the argument may be a floating-point number to indicate a more precise sleep time (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook admits that it has not discussed the function yet and says that it introduces a one-tenth-of-a-second pause in the program (Sweigart, 2025).

Without a pause, a program that prints a line in every pass of a loop would run so fast that the whole animation would fly past in an instant. A short pause gives the eye time to follow the pattern. The function is also used wherever a program has to wait, for example between attempts to reach something that is not ready.
