Both animation programs call time.sleep(0.1) in every pass of their main loop, after the print call. The function belongs to the time module, so the program needs the line import time first, and the call is written with the module name in front, like the other module functions of this chapter.

The call returns None, as print does, and it returns after the pause. A program that measures the time with time.perf_counter() around time.sleep(0.1) finds that at least a tenth of a second passed and, on an ordinary run, well under a second. The reference says that perf_counter includes time elapsed during sleep (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The pause is not exact. The reference says that the suspension time may be longer than requested by an arbitrary amount, because of the scheduling of other activity in the system (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program should not use the pause as a clock. The pause also does not block Ctrl-C: when an interrupt arrives during a five second sleep, the sleep ends early with KeyboardInterrupt, and in the check the program ended in under three seconds.

nodes.definition: A function from the time module that pauses the program for the given number of seconds.

nodes.label: KeyboardInterrupt
nodes.body: KeyboardInterrupt is the exception that Python raises when the user presses Ctrl-C while a program is running. The textbook says exactly this: when the user presses CTRL-C while a Python program is running, Python raises the KeyboardInterrupt exception (Sweigart, 2025). The library reference words it as raised when the user hits the interrupt key, normally Control-C or Delete (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: KeyboardInterrupt is the exception that Python raises when the user presses Ctrl-C while a program is running. The textbook says exactly this: when the user presses CTRL-C while a Python program is running, Python raises the KeyboardInterrupt exception (Sweigart, 2025). The library reference words it as raised when the user hits the interrupt key, normally Control-C or Delete (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A program that never ends by itself needs a way out. The user can always end it with the interrupt key, but if the exception is not caught, the textbook says the program crashes with an ugly error message (Sweigart, 2025). Catching it lets the program stop in the way the programmer chooses.

In the zigzag and spike programs, the whole loop is inside a try clause, and the except clause at the end names KeyboardInterrupt and calls sys.exit(). When an interrupt arrives while the program sleeps, the handler runs and prints its message. The check in this corpus starts a second program that is sleeping, sends it the interrupt and observes that its handler ran.

The reference notes that during execution, a check for interrupts is made regularly (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Where the interrupt is noticed, it is raised like any other exception, so it travels outwards through the frames until a handler for KeyboardInterrupt is found. The animation programs put the try statement outside the loop, so the handler is found no matter in which pass the key was pressed.

KeyboardInterrupt is not an Exception. The reference says that it inherits from BaseException so as to not be accidentally caught by code that catches Exception and thus prevent the interpreter from exiting (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler written as except Exception does not catch the interrupt, and the interrupt passes on to an outer KeyboardInterrupt handler. A handler for BaseException would catch it, which is why that class is the wrong target for a handler meant for ordinary errors.

nodes.definition: The exception raised when the user presses Ctrl-C; the animation programs catch it to stop cleanly.

nodes.label: The sys.exit function
nodes.body: The function sys.exit ends a program. The library reference says that it raises a SystemExit exception, signaling an intention to exit the interpreter (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook's animation programs call it from the except clause for KeyboardInterrupt, so that the program ends without an error message (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The function sys.exit ends a program. The library reference says that it raises a SystemExit exception, signaling an intention to exit the interpreter (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook's animation programs call it from the except clause for KeyboardInterrupt, so that the program ends without an error message (Sweigart, 2025).

A program needs a deliberate way to finish from the middle of its code, for instance when it has detected a problem or when the user asks to stop. The optional argument tells the operating system and other programs whether the run succeeded, which matters as soon as a program is started by another one.

Called with no argument, sys.exit() ends the program with exit status 0, which the reference calls successful termination. Called with an integer such as 2, the status is 2, and any nonzero value is considered abnormal termination. Called with a string, as in sys.exit('bye'), the string is printed to the error stream, the channel on which error messages are written, and the exit status is 1. The reference calls the last form a quick way to exit a program when an error occurs (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Since the function only raises an exception, the program does not end at once: the exception travels outwards like any other. The reference says that cleanup actions specified by finally clauses of try statements are honored, and that it is possible to intercept the exit attempt at an outer level (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler for SystemExit can read the status from the code attribute of the exception, which is None when no argument was given, and the program then keeps running.

A handler for Exception does not intercept the exit, because SystemExit inherits from BaseException so that it is not accidentally caught by code that catches Exception (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The reverse mistake is easy too: a program that catches SystemExit and does nothing with it will not end, which is what the reference means by intercepting the exit attempt.

nodes.definition: A function from the sys module that ends the program by raising SystemExit; an argument sets the exit status.

nodes.label: Practice programs
nodes.body: The textbook ends the chapter with practice programs: tasks for the reader to write without a model solution (Sweigart, 2025). The two tasks in this chapter build on one another. The first asks for a function named collatz and a program that calls it, and the second adds try and except statements to that program.

paras.text: The textbook ends the chapter with practice programs: tasks for the reader to write without a model solution (Sweigart, 2025). The two tasks in this chapter build on one another. The first asks for a function named collatz and a program that calls it, and the second adds try and except statements to that program.

Practice programs turn the chapter's concepts into habits. The first needs a function with a parameter and a return value, the second needs error handling around user input, so between them they use almost every idea of the chapter.

The sections of this group present the two tasks, say what each one needs from the chapter, and point out where the textbook's wording needs a correction or a limit that the reader would otherwise find the hard way.

Each task has an edge that the textbook's wording leaves open. The Collatz sequence from 3 is 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, so the function is called seven times before the value reaches 1, while a start of 1 yields no further numbers at all, which a loop written to test before it runs handles and a loop written to run at least once does not (Sweigart, 2025). The handler of the second task catches the ValueError that int raises for text that is not a whole number, since int('hello') raises ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'.

nodes.label: Collatz sequence
nodes.body: The Collatz sequence is the first practice program. The textbook asks for a function named collatz that has one parameter named number: if number is even, the function should print number // 2 and return this value, and if number is odd, it should print and return 3 * number + 1 (Sweigart, 2025). The program then keeps calling the function on the result until it returns 1.

paras.text: The Collatz sequence is the first practice program. The textbook asks for a function named collatz that has one parameter named number: if number is even, the function should print number // 2 and return this value, and if number is odd, it should print and return 3 * number + 1 (Sweigart, 2025). The program then keeps calling the function on the result until it returns 1.

It practises the main ideas of the chapter in a few lines: a parameter, a return value that is used in the next call, and a loop that stops on a condition. It is also a famous problem. The textbook calls it the simplest impossible math problem, and says that even mathematicians are not sure why the sequence reaches 1 (Sweigart, 2025).

Starting at 3, the program prints 3 10 5 16 8 4 2 1, as in the textbook's sample, and the rule used is the same on every step: 3 is odd, so the next value is 3 * 3 + 1, which is 10; 10 is even, so the next is 5. Counting the steps, the start 3 reaches 1 in 7 steps and its largest value is 16, while the start 27 needs 111 steps and reaches 9232 on the way.

A number is even if number % 2 == 0, which is the hint the textbook gives. The program stores the returned value back in the same variable, n = collatz(n), and the loop condition is n != 1. To print all the values on one line, the print calls need the named parameter end=' ' so that a space replaces the newline. The textbook's hint names sep=' ' for this, but sep only changes what goes between several values in one call, and with a single value in each call it changes nothing: printing 3 and then 10 with sep=' ' still gives two lines.

The textbook says that the sequence works for any integer, but the loop does not end for all of them. For 0 the rule gives 0 // 2, which is 0 again, and for -1 it gives -2 and then -1 again, so after 1000 steps the values are still 0 and -1 and a program that waits for 1 would never finish. The sequence is a question about positive integers. Input from the user should therefore also be checked for being greater than zero, not only for being a number.

nodes.definition: A function that prints and returns number // 2 for an even number and 3 * number + 1 for an odd one, called until the value is 1.

io.code: (lambda n: n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1)(3)

nodes.label: Input validation
nodes.body: Input validation means checking what the user typed before using it. The second practice task asks the reader to add try and except statements to the previous project to detect whether the user entered a non-integer string (Sweigart, 2025). The tool is the conversion function int, which converts text to an integer and, in the textbook's words, normally raises a ValueError if it is passed a non-integer string, as in int('puppy').

paras.text: Input validation means checking what the user typed before using it. The second practice task asks the reader to add try and except statements to the previous project to detect whether the user entered a non-integer string (Sweigart, 2025). The tool is the conversion function int, which converts text to an integer and, in the textbook's words, normally raises a ValueError if it is passed a non-integer string, as in int('puppy').

The user is the least predictable part of a program. The program of the previous section works when the user types a number and ends with a traceback when the user types a word. A handler around the conversion turns that traceback into a message the user can act on, and a program can then ask again.

For int('puppy') the handler receives a ValueError whose text is invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'puppy'. In the textbook's wording, the except clause then prints a message to the user saying they must enter an integer. A small function can wrap the idea: to_int returns int(text) inside a try clause, prints You must enter an integer. in the except clause for ValueError, and so returns 42 for '42' and None for 'puppy'.

Only the line that does the conversion belongs in the try clause, and the exception type to name is the one that int raises. The None from the failed conversion is the value Python supplies when a function ends without a return statement, which means the code that uses the result must be ready for it.

The handler catches only ValueError. A user who just presses Enter gives int an empty string, which is also a ValueError, but a value of another type, such as None passed by mistake, would raise a TypeError and the program would still crash. Also, as the previous section noted, an integer is not always a valid input: 0 and negative integers pass the conversion and still never reach 1 in the sequence.

nodes.definition: Wrapping the conversion of the user's text in try and except, so that text that is not an integer produces a message instead of a crash.

nodes.label: Modern practice
nodes.body: Modern practice is the part of the chapter that goes beyond the textbook's list of topics to what a programmer needs around functions today. It has two groups. The first, Annotations, is about the notes that can be written on a function's parameters and result, and about the way Python 3.14 stores them. The second, Style, is about the habits that make a function easy to use and to read: treating it as a black box, naming it well and commenting it.

paras.text: Modern practice is the part of the chapter that goes beyond the textbook's list of topics to what a programmer needs around functions today. It has two groups. The first, Annotations, is about the notes that can be written on a function's parameters and result, and about the way Python 3.14 stores them. The second, Style, is about the habits that make a function easy to use and to read: treating it as a black box, naming it well and commenting it.

An advanced course reads code written by other people, and that code uses all of these. Annotations appear in the signature of almost every function in a modern library, and the change in Python 3.14 decides whether code that uses them runs at all on a given release. Style is not decoration: the black box idea is the reason that functions are useful, and PEP 8 is the style guide for the code of Python's standard library (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

A function from a current library may look like def add(a: int, b: int = 0) -> int:, with a note after each parameter and one after the arrow. The same function is used by its callers without reading its body, is named in lowercase words joined by underscores, and has comments only where the code needs them.

The sections follow the order in which a reader meets the ideas: first what an annotation is and what Python does with it, then the 3.14 change that postpones the evaluation, then the three style topics. Each section marks the release in which its behaviour holds.

Annotations are the area where releases differ most, since the behaviour of a definition with an undefined name in its annotation changed between Python 3.12 and 3.14. The sections state the release for every claim.

nodes.label: Annotations
nodes.body: An annotation is an expression written next to a parameter or after the arrow that follows the parameter list. PEP 3107 defines function annotations, both for parameters and return values, as completely optional and as nothing more than a way of associating arbitrary Python expressions with various parts of a function at compile-time (Winter and Lownds, 2006). The usual expression is the name of a type, such as int.

paras.text: An annotation is an expression written next to a parameter or after the arrow that follows the parameter list. PEP 3107 defines function annotations, both for parameters and return values, as completely optional and as nothing more than a way of associating arbitrary Python expressions with various parts of a function at compile-time (Winter and Lownds, 2006). The usual expression is the name of a type, such as int.

A note on what a function expects and gives back is information for the reader, for the editor and for tools that check programs, and it needs no comment to keep it in step with the code. Python 3.14 changes when the notes are evaluated, which is why this group has two sections: the notation itself and its newest behaviour.

The first section describes the notation and what Python does with it, which is almost nothing. The second describes deferred evaluation, adopted in Python 3.14, under which a note may name something that does not exist yet.

That the notes are stored and not checked can be confirmed in two lines. A function defined as def twice(n: int) -> int keeps its notes in twice.__annotations__, which reports the parameter and the return both as int, and yet twice('ab') runs and gives back 'abab', because an annotation carries no check with it (Winter and Lownds, 2006). Under the deferred evaluation adopted in Python 3.14 the expressions are not evaluated until something asks for them, so an annotation may name a class that the file defines further down.

nodes.label: Function annotation
nodes.body: A function annotation is a note attached to a parameter or to the return value. For a parameter it follows the name after a colon, and for the result it follows an arrow made of a hyphen and a greater-than sign, placed before the colon that ends the def line. PEP 3107 gives the pseudo-grammar of a parameter as the name, then an optional expression after a colon, then an optional default value, so the note always comes before the default (Winter and Lownds, 2006).

paras.text: A function annotation is a note attached to a parameter or to the return value. For a parameter it follows the name after a colon, and for the result it follows an arrow made of a hyphen and a greater-than sign, placed before the colon that ends the def line. PEP 3107 gives the pseudo-grammar of a parameter as the name, then an optional expression after a colon, then an optional default value, so the note always comes before the default (Winter and Lownds, 2006).

Annotations let a function state its contract in its own signature. A reader sees at once that add expects two integers and gives back an integer, without opening the body. Editors and checking programs can use the same notes to warn about a call that does not fit.

For def add(a: int, b: int = 0) -> int: return a + b, Python stores the notes and add.__annotations__ shows that a, b and the result are all marked with the type int. Calling add(2, 3) gives 5. Calling add('x', 'y') also works and gives 'xy', although the notes say int.

PEP 3107 states that, by itself, Python does not attach any particular meaning or significance to annotations; it simply makes the expressions available in the function's __annotations__ attribute, and the only way that annotations take on meaning is when they are interpreted by third-party libraries (Winter and Lownds, 2006). The attribute pairs each parameter name with its note, and the note for the result is stored under the name return. In Python 3.12 all annotation expressions were evaluated when the function definition was executed, just like default values.

A note is not a check. The call add('x', 'y') above shows that Python runs the function whatever the notes say. A lambda expression cannot carry annotations, which the language reference states and the lambda section of this chapter shows. And since the notes are real expressions, a wrong or misspelled name inside one is a real error in Python 3.12, which is the problem the next section addresses.

nodes.definition: A note on a parameter or on the result, written after a colon or an arrow; Python stores it but does not enforce it.

nodes.label: Deferred annotations
nodes.body: Deferred evaluation means that Python 3.14 does not work out an annotation when the function is defined, but stores it and works it out only when somebody asks. What's New in Python 3.14 states it: the annotations on functions, classes and modules are no longer evaluated eagerly; instead they are stored in special-purpose annotate functions and evaluated only when necessary (Python Software Foundation, 2026). PEP 649 proposed the change (Hastings, 2021).

paras.text: Deferred evaluation means that Python 3.14 does not work out an annotation when the function is defined, but stores it and works it out only when somebody asks. What's New in Python 3.14 states it: the annotations on functions, classes and modules are no longer evaluated eagerly; instead they are stored in special-purpose annotate functions and evaluated only when necessary (Python Software Foundation, 2026). PEP 649 proposed the change (Hastings, 2021).

Before the change, a note that named something defined later in the file had to be written as a string, so that its evaluation would not fail. What's New says that it is no longer necessary to enclose annotations in strings if they contain forward references (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The change also lowers the cost of defining a function, since its notes are not evaluated until they are wanted.

The line def f(x: Undefined) -> Missing: return x defines a function with two names that do not exist. Under Python 3.12 the definition itself fails with NameError: name 'Undefined' is not defined. Under Python 3.14 the definition succeeds, and f(3) returns 3. Asking for f.__annotations__ then raises the NameError, because that is the moment when the names are evaluated.

The standard library module annotationlib reads the notes in one of three formats. The VALUE format evaluates them, as earlier releases did and fails on an undefined name; the FORWARDREF format replaces undefined names with special markers; and the STRING format returns the annotations as strings (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For the function above, the FORWARDREF format gives entries for x and the result without raising an error, and the STRING format gives the text Undefined for x and Missing for the result. Under Python 3.12 the module annotationlib does not exist.

The change is a reason to read the release notes before moving a program between versions. A program written for 3.14 that relies on an annotation naming something defined later runs only on 3.14 and later; run by 3.12 it stops at the def line. What's New adds that in the majority of cases code will continue working as-is (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and code that reads __annotations__ directly is the code that needs a second look.

nodes.definition: Since Python 3.14 a function's annotations are not evaluated at definition, so names that do not exist yet can be used and are looked up only on request.

nodes.label: Style
nodes.body: Style means the habits of writing and using a function that go beyond making it work. The textbook has one such idea, the black box, and PEP 8 is the style guide for the code in Python's standard library (Van Rossum et al., 2001). This group treats three habits: using a function without reading it, naming it and commenting it.

paras.text: Style means the habits of writing and using a function that go beyond making it work. The textbook has one such idea, the black box, and PEP 8 is the style guide for the code in Python's standard library (Van Rossum et al., 2001). This group treats three habits: using a function without reading it, naming it and commenting it.

How a function is meant to be used matters as much as how it is written. A program is read many more times than it is written, and each habit reduces the amount that a reader has to hold in mind: the black box lets the reader skip the body, a good name tells what the function does, and a good comment explains what the code cannot say.

The three sections apply to the same small functions that the chapter has used: a function that doubles a number, a function that divides, a function that prints a greeting. Each states the rule of the style guide or the textbook that supports it, and shows what happens when the rule is broken.

Each habit rests on a rule that can be quoted. The style guide asks that a function name be lowercase with words separated by underscores, so send_message is the recommended form and the mixed-case spelling is kept only where it is already the prevailing style of the code around it (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The black box is the same idea from the reader's side: a call such as divide(42, 2) can be used on the strength of its name, its parameters and its return value, and the body only has to be opened when one of those three fails to answer the question.

nodes.label: Function as a black box
nodes.body: A black box is a function used through its inputs and its output alone. The textbook says that often all you need to know about a function are its inputs, the parameters, and its output value, and that thinking of a function in this high-level way is called treating it as a black box (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter summary repeats the idea: the inputs are in the form of parameters, the outputs are return values, and the code in them does not affect variables in other functions.

paras.text: A black box is a function used through its inputs and its output alone. The textbook says that often all you need to know about a function are its inputs, the parameters, and its output value, and that thinking of a function in this high-level way is called treating it as a black box (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter summary repeats the idea: the inputs are in the form of parameters, the outputs are return values, and the code in them does not affect variables in other functions.

The idea is what makes large programs possible. The textbook calls it fundamental to modern programming, because later chapters show modules with functions written by other people, which can be used without knowing how they work (Sweigart, 2025). A reader who may rely on a function's inputs and output only has far less to understand than one who must follow every line.

In the program x = 1, then def f(): x = 99 and return x * 2, then print(f(), x), the function returns 198 and the global x is still 1. The assignment inside f created a local variable and left the global one alone, so nothing outside f can tell how f got its result.

The idea rests on the scope rules of this chapter. Variables assigned in a function are local, so they disappear when the call ends, and a function that has no global statement cannot change a global variable. What goes in is the arguments, and what comes out is the return value. The textbook adds that because writing functions without global variables is encouraged, you usually do not have to worry about the function's code interacting with the rest of your program (Sweigart, 2025).

The box is only as sealed as its author made it. A function that uses a global statement, or that reads a global variable that others may change, depends on something that is not in its parameters, and then the call f(2) no longer says everything about what the result will be. Printing instead of returning is the other leak: the output reaches a person but cannot be used by the caller.

nodes.definition: A function can be treated as a black box: its parameters go in, its return value comes out, and its local variables affect nothing else.

nodes.label: Function naming
nodes.body: A function name is an identifier chosen by the programmer, and PEP 8 has a rule for it. Function names should be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary to improve readability, and variable names follow the same convention; mixedCase is allowed only in contexts where that is already the prevailing style (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The chapter's own names, such as say_hello_to, follow it.

paras.text: A function name is an identifier chosen by the programmer, and PEP 8 has a rule for it. Function names should be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary to improve readability, and variable names follow the same convention; mixedCase is allowed only in contexts where that is already the prevailing style (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The chapter's own names, such as say_hello_to, follow it.

A function is called many more times than it is defined, so its name is what most readers see. A name that says what the function does lets a reader follow a program without opening the functions, which is the black box idea in practice. A common convention also lets a reader guess the name of a function, without looking it up.

Python tells names apart by case. If the program defines Hello and then calls hello(), the call fails with NameError: name 'hello' is not defined, since no function with that exact name exists. A name that is a reserved keyword is rejected before the program runs: the line def = 3 gives SyntaxError: invalid syntax.

PEP 8 also covers the case in which the best name is a keyword. If a function argument's name clashes with a reserved keyword, it is generally better to append a single trailing underscore rather than use an abbreviation or spelling corruption, so class_ is better than clss (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The check keyword.iskeyword tells whether a name is reserved: it says yes for def and for None and for lambda, and no for print, which is an ordinary function.

The guide is a convention, not a rule enforced by Python: a function named Hello works exactly as well as one named hello, provided the calls use the same spelling. PEP 8 also warns that the guide is about consistency, and has a section titled A Foolish Consistency is the Hobgoblin of Little Minds, which says that in some cases the guide does not apply. The guide itself says that consistency within a project is more important than consistency with the guide (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

nodes.definition: PEP 8 asks for lowercase function names with words separated by underscores; Python tells names apart by case, so the call must match the definition.

nodes.label: Comment
nodes.body: A comment is a note for the human reader that Python does not execute. The tutorial says that comments in Python start with the hash character, #, and extend to the end of the physical line, that a comment may appear at the start of a line or following whitespace or code, and that since comments are to clarify code and are not interpreted by Python, they may be omitted when typing in examples (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A comment is a note for the human reader that Python does not execute. The tutorial says that comments in Python start with the hash character, #, and extend to the end of the physical line, that a comment may appear at the start of a line or following whitespace or code, and that since comments are to clarify code and are not interpreted by Python, they may be omitted when typing in examples (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Code says what it does; a comment can say why. The textbook's examples use comments in this way, such as the one inside the try clause that tells the reader that any code in the block that causes ZeroDivisionError will not crash the program (Sweigart, 2025). PEP 8 adds a warning about the cost: comments that contradict the code are worse than no comments, and keeping them up to date when the code changes is a priority (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

In the line print('# not a comment')  # this is a comment, the first hash is inside quotes and is part of the text, and the second one starts a comment. The program prints # not a comment. A line that starts with # is skipped completely, so a statement placed behind a hash, such as # print('hidden'), does not run.

PEP 8 distinguishes two kinds. Block comments generally apply to some or all of the code that follows them and are indented to the same level as that code; each line starts with a # and a single space. Inline comments are on the same line as a statement, are separated from it by at least two spaces, and should be used sparingly (Van Rossum et al., 2001). Comments should be complete sentences.

A comment that restates the code adds noise. PEP 8 gives the example x = x + 1 with the comment Increment x, and calls such comments unnecessary and in fact distracting, whereas a comment such as Compensate for border is useful (Van Rossum et al., 2001). A hash inside a string literal does not start a comment, which is the mistake the example above demonstrates.

nodes.definition: Text that starts with a hash character and runs to the end of the line; Python ignores it.
